items.title: Supporting Materials for Observability in Agentic Coding
items.abstract: This record contains supporting research materials for the thesis “Observability in Agentic Coding: Evaluating Practitioner Requirements and Existing Tools.” The study draws on 12 semi-structured practitioner interviews and thematic analysis to identify ten observability requirements. Materials included in this record are described in the file list. Interview recordings and any personal or identifiable information are excluded from public access unless sharing has been explicitly authorised.
authors: Dhanush Janapareddy; Gubala Haribabu Laasya Sai
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

items.title: MetaMatch: Reconciling Metadata for Aggregating Music Difficulty Annotations
items.abstract: The inconsistency of metadata across sources is a persistent problem for large-scale music research. The variety of approaches to documenting even basic elements such as artists’ names and work titles makes it difficult to aggregate data across different sources. This paper presents a comparative analysis of approaches to this problem, combining the OpenRefine Reconciliation pipeline with LLM-based strategies for entity matching. We also explore one potential application of this pipeline in sheet music difficulty classification. By gathering difficulty labels from established music exam board syllabi and matching them to corresponding IMSLP entries, we link expert difficulty annotations to sheet music available through IMSLP for automatic sheet music difficulty classification. The resulting piano dataset consists of 7,737 repertoire-list entries, of which 2,389 are automatically matched to 1,210 distinct IMSLP work identifiers. Our method produces data that combine high-quality expert annotations with the scale more typically associated with crowd-sourced corpora, and can be extended to additional instruments. We release the matching pipeline, dataset, and code at https://meganelisabethfinch.github.io/metamatch to support further work on cross-corpus music analysis, both for this use case and for the many others which depend on robust metadata alignment at scale.

items.title: Mitigating Agentic Deception via Evaluation-Side Partially Observable Games
items.abstract: As large language models become more capable agents, they can exhibit deceptive behaviors, cheating human for higher rewards while appearing helpful. We attribute this failure to evaluation-side partial observability, where models are evaluated mainly from final outcome, without checking the faithfulness of underlying reasoning, tool use, and environmental effects. Prior mitigations address this partial observability by predefined evaluator latent belief space or one-shot monitoring, which do not extend to free-form language space and vulnerable to stronger deceptions that evade simple monitoring. In this work, we formulate deception mitigation as an Evaluation-Side Partially Observable Extensive Form Game (e-PoG), a max-min framework in which an agent maximizes reward, a monitor minimizes the agent's payoff by exposing deception from the full interaction trajectory, and a fixed verifier validates the monitor's claims and converts them into penalties. We define the solution concept as a Subgame-Perfect Oversight Equilibrium (SPOE) between agent and monitor, and prove its existence in finite games. With a perfect verifier, every SPOE is faithful; with an imperfect verifier, the guarantee persists if verifier errors do not reverse the ranking of monitor actions. To achieve faithful SPOE, we derive a two-timescale policy gradient algorithm and enhance the pipeline empirically with NLI verification and deterministic checks. Experiments with Gemma3-4B-IT and Qwen3-4B/8B on Agentic Role-Playing, SearchQA, and WebShop show that e-PoG mitigates multiple emergent deception modes, outperforming the strongest baselines by 26.0% in deception mitigation and by up to 39.8% in task success. These gains persist under weak-to-strong supervision. Code is available at https://github.com/Toyoid/deceptive-agent.

items.title: Inference Validation for Regulated AI: Building a Decision Pipeline on NVIDIA AIPerf
items.abstract: Deploying large language models in regulated industries requires more than picking the fastest inference engine: it requires evidence that a configuration meets contractual and legal obligations before it serves a single customer request. We describe Runway, an internal validation harness built at MasterControl that builds a governed decision pipeline around NVIDIA AIPerf. The key insight is separating concerns: AIPerf provides the trusted measurement, while Runway provides the experiment design that comes before it and the compliance, cost, and audit decisions that come after. We describe the architecture and the storage model that makes caching and audit one mechanism. We report three findings from Runway sweeps: TensorRT-LLM and vLLM rankings invert with concurrency; a newer, pricier GPU instance can be the cheaper one per request; and speculative decoding behaves differently across engines under load, so engine configuration can outweigh engine choice.

items.title: Will AI mess my RTL? A snapshot-based approach to verifying AI-written RTL
items.abstract: With the growing interest in using AI (Artificial Intelligence) for RTL (Register-Transfer Level) hardware development, robust and comprehensive verification has become more important than ever. As Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly assist in creating and modifying RTL designs, ensuring that these changes preserve existing functionality is paramount for building trust in AI-driven workflows. We present SVApshot, a fully automated framework that leverages LLMs to generate and systematically attempt to correct SystemVerilog Assertions (SVA) for RTL modules, completely removing the human from the generation loop. SVApshot introduces a novel snapshot methodology that captures the current functionality of a design as a comprehensive set of formal assertions, creating a regression suite for validating future changes--whether made by humans or AI. The framework features automated duplicate detection, assertion set expansion, and iterative repair of failing assertions using LLM-guided debugging with formal verification feedback. Our experimental evaluation across diverse RTL modules demonstrates high coverage for complex modules, with successful detection of both manually-injected and AI-introduced bugs. Additionally, this framework opens the door for automatic generation of formal testbenches to benchmark LLMs for hardware design, moving beyond binary pass/fail metrics towards nuanced assertion-based scoring.

items.title: Multi-Agent Screening: What Agreement and Acceptance Cannot Tell You
items.abstract: When AI agents screen items for a costly human assessor, as in agentic search, e-discovery and AI reviewing of papers, only what they pass gets judged. We show what each kind of evidence can establish about their errors, even with unlimited data. Agreement shows that agents concur, not that they are right, however many there are. Acceptance by the assessor gives precision but only a lower bound on recall. Knowing which agents found which relevant items gives an upper bound on recall if agents' finds are not negatively correlated, and caps what one more agent can add if agents are interchangeable. Without assumptions about the agents, recall can be pinned down only by judging items they did not pass: a random sample of these estimates how many relevant items were missed, to any chosen accuracy, and the sample needed does not grow with the number of agents.

items.title: Beyond Sunny Skies: Using Large Language Models to Predict Urban Traffic in Adverse Weather
items.abstract: Urban traffic flow prediction is a cornerstone of intelligent transportation systems, yet accurate forecasting under adverse weather conditions remains a significant challenge. Existing data-driven models, while effective for routine patterns, often struggle with the sparse data and complex non-linear shifts associated with rare meteorological events. These methods typically treat environmental contexts as shallow numerical features, failing to capture the underlying semantic reasoning-why and how specific adverse conditions alter mobility behaviors across regions with different functional compositions. To address this limitation, we propose Multi-STG, a unified framework that integrates Large Language Model (LLM)-derived semantic priors with graph-based spatiotemporal learning. Multi-STG introduces an LLM-empowered semantic enhancement module that transforms comprehensive context descriptions such as weather, POIs, and holidays into high-level semantic embeddings, effectively providing a knowledge-driven complement to data scarcity. Furthermore, we design a multimodal attentional fusion mechanism to dynamically weigh heterogeneous inputs and a semantic-enhanced prediction head with gated residual calibration to robustly adjust forecasts based on semantic guidance. Extensive experiments on real-world multi-city private car datasets demonstrate that Multi-STG outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, reducing MAE by 11.82\% on average relative to the strongest baseline across three cities, while maintaining stable performance under sparse and non-stationary conditions.

items.title: Out-of-the-Box Tabular Foundation Models for Bayesian Optimization in Materials Discovery
items.abstract: Bayesian optimization is widely used in active learning loops for materials science. Gaussian processes serve as the de-facto surrogate model family, but require task-dependent kernel choices and can lack the modeling capacity for complex relationships. Tabular foundation models (TFMs) have recently emerged as the state-of-the-art for predictive tasks on structured data, without requiring bespoke kernels or hyperparameter tuning. We evaluate two TFMs, TabPFN and TabICL, as out-of-the-box surrogate models on two standard materials science benchmarks, comparing against a large field of baselines encompassing Gaussian processes, random forests, and CatBoost. Our findings indicate that TFMs are highly competitive surrogate models across the two benchmarks, without task-specific training for active learning or GP kernel selection. Our results motivate developing TFMs further as surrogates for active learning in materials discovery.

items.title: Schottky barrier height modulation and memristive behavior in a mechanically exfoliated $MoS_2$ flake with multiple lateral electrodes
items.abstract: Van de Waals materials possess great potential as core active materials for novel electronics, optoelectronics, and sensing applications. In particular, transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) and other low-dimensional materials, such as hexagonal boron nitride and binary oxides exhibit memristive behavior, making them attractive candidates as building blocks for resistive memories and neuromorphic computing devices. In this work, we investigate two-terminal lateral memristors based on mechanically exfoliated few layer $MoS_2$ flakes. We study the influence of the Schottky barrier height (SBH) as a function of the contact area. We report different SBHs from 60 meV up to 208 meV in the same $MoS_2$ flake and analyze the effect of the SBH in the memristive-like $J-V_{DS}$ curves and the observed non-volatile/volatile resistance switching. Our results highlight the importance of contact engineering to obtain different memristive properties in $MoS_2$-based devices.

items.title: To SIMD or Not to SIMD: Comparing RVV vs. CGRA SoCs for Non-Linear Functions in AI
items.abstract: Non-linear functions are an important class of operations in modern large language models. However, chip vendors building for AI have so far relied on traditional vector or scalar processing units for non-linear functions. The performance of these units has not kept pace with matrix multiplication units (MMUs), which can be found in both high-performance and edge-computing devices from almost every vendor. Reconfigurable units such as FPGAs and CGRAs have been proposed in the literature, but have not been systematically compared with traditional units backed by MMUs. In this paper, we build two SoCs: one using an RVV vector processor and the other using a latency-insensitive (\emph{elastic}) CGRA, both coupled with an MMU and driven by a single-core CPU. We then propose mappings for common feed-forward networks on our SoCs and find that the CGRA reaches a maximum speedup in clock cycles of 7.12x over RVV on the activation stage of simple point-wise non-linear functions like SiLU, whereas the RVV reaches a maximum speedup of \textbf{9.8x} over the CGRA on complex non-linear functions such as $\mathrm{softmax}$. Over the enclosing feed-forward block the corresponding maxima are 3.16x and 4.24x.

items.title: Detecting Shadow AI: Unsanctioned LLM Agents on Enterprise Endpoints: A Taxonomy, an Open Detector and a Controlled Evaluation
items.abstract: Shadow IT, the use of technology that the IT organisation has not approved, is a long-standing governance problem. We argue that autonomous AI agents can make it grow much faster: agents make building tools nearly free, act with their user's privileges, and leave behind scripts, automations and MCP servers that are themselves unsanctioned. A simple compounding model shows that, under its assumptions, shadow IT grows exponentially once agentic artifacts reproduce faster than the organisation retires them; retiring them starts with detecting them. We then ask whether unsanctioned agents can be detected on Windows endpoints. We propose a taxonomy of nine classes of agents and six layers of endpoint footprint, and argue that rules based only on the structure of processes and connections cannot separate an agent from its behavioural twin, the same program talking to a non-AI service. We present Agent Detector, an open-source Windows detector that anchors behaviour to the identity of the remote service and correlates it with configuration, installation and execution history, using a catalog of 39 tools and 184 LLM endpoint entries; it informs users through a notice they must acknowledge instead of blocking. On a controlled bench of 12 synthetic agents, 3 AI components and 9 benign workloads, repeated 5 times on one workstation, two behavioural rules flagged every behavioural twin, while Agent Detector flagged none and detected every agent in the majority of runs. Its limits are temporal: a connection to a provider behind a shared content-delivery network is attributable only while the DNS cache holds the provider's name, one to five minutes, and an intermittent agent was seen by about one scan in three. A scan costs about 154 ms. The bench is too small to rank detectors; it maps what each kind of evidence can see: unsanctioned agents can be partly detected, and not by behaviour alone.

items.title: Depth as a Candidate Source: Portfolio Allocation for Recurrent Test-Time Scaling in Large Language Models
items.abstract: Recurrent latent reasoning in large lanugage models (LLMs) scales test-time computation by increasing recurrent depth, naturally framing inference as a problem of deciding when to stop. We identify a previously overlooked limitation of this single-depth view through systematic preliminary analysis: deeper recurrence can lose correct solutions found at shallower depths, while depth-specific success sets remain broadly non-nested even after controlling for marginal accuracy. This suggests that depth determines not only computation cost, but also access to distinct candidate solutions. Motivated by this finding, we propose Depth Portfolio Allocation (DPA), which reformulates recurrent test-time scaling as budgeted allocation across depth-specific candidate sources. DPA supports both fixed portfolios and feedback-guided sequential allocation under a shared inference budget. Experiments on GSM8K, SVAMP, MultiArith, and MBPP show that mixed-depth portfolios expand oracle coverage under matched candidate counts and nominal costs, while feedback-guided allocation generally matches or improves uniform allocation and can reduce computation in high-budget settings. Code and data are avaible at : https://anonymous.4open.science/r/LLM-latent-B7BC/.

items.title: Learning Evidence-Grounded Reasoning for Context-Aware Time Series Forecasting
items.abstract: LLM-driven time series forecasting has become increasingly promising by leveraging contextual features to generate future values directly or refine forecast priors. However, incorporating contextual features alone does not ensure that models can identify which features matter for forecasting and understand what they suggest about future dynamics. We argue that the fundamental challenge is how to extract predictive evidence from contextual features and when and how to leverage it to guide forecasting decisions. In this paper, we propose CastReasoner, an evidence-grounded reasoning model for context-aware time series forecasting. Specifically, CastReasoner uses a structured chain of thought (CoT) to extract predictive evidence from contextual features, infer the future dynamics suggested by this evidence, and assess these dynamics against the forecast prior to guide adaptive forecasting decisions. To enable this capability, we design a reasoning-centric two-stage post-training framework including supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL). First, we synthesize reasoning trajectories through controllable multi-teacher guidance and select high-quality ones using a novel student-aware difficulty metric. Second, we design fine-grained multi-objective rewards to further improve reasoning and forecasting. To address heterogeneous learning needs across domains in both stages, we introduce a convergence-guided data balancing strategy. Through this two-stage training, CastReasoner improves both reasoning quality and predictive accuracy. Extensive experiments across multi-domain forecasting benchmarks demonstrate that CastReasoner achieves superior forecasting performance.

items.title: A Cost That Practice Accuracy Hides: Worked Solutions in Self-Generated Training Data and the Compositional Use of New Rules
items.abstract: A worked solution can make self-generated training targets shorter and cheaper, but accuracy on the practiced operation may hide how well a model can reuse newly learned rules. We study this choice in a 2B-parameter reasoning model learning two invented quantitative rules. The model generates targets from a rule sheet alone or from the sheet plus a program-written worked solution; targets are accepted for final-answer correctness, and the support is removed for fine-tuning and evaluation. Training questions request forward use in one segment; composition requires sequential reuse of the same rule across two segments. After six passes, using a program-checked numerical signature, sheet-only targets lead by 24.3 percentage points (95% item-bootstrap CI 14.6-34.0) on composition in a prospective test. On unseen argument values, observed forward accuracy is identical (87.5% each), but composition accuracy is 58.3% versus 23.6%, a 34.7-point gap (25.7-43.8). An independently sampled second target-bank pair repeats the direction (+14.6 points, 2.1-26.0). Ten passes on the shorter worked-solution targets, approximately matching the domain tokens of six sheet-only passes while changing other training quantities, narrow the gap to 16.3 points (6.3-26.7) in the first bank pair and 6.2 points (-6.3 to 18.8) in the second, where the pre-specified test does not hold. At six passes each, the worked-solution policy uses fewer capture tokens and less update time, yet the trained models use 2.6 times as many generated tokens per composition success under the numerical signature (2.1 times in the second bank pair). Choosing a capture context therefore requires testing how the new rules are reused, alongside the inference cost of those uses, rather than relying on forward accuracy alone.

items.title: PARIS: A multi-agent LLM framework for end-to-end, PRISMA-guided systematic literature reviews with pre-synthesis corpus quality assessment
items.abstract: Systematic literature reviews (SRs) remain slow and labor-intensive, and most automation tools address single stages of the workflow. We present PARIS (PRISMA Agentic Research Intelligence System), an open-source framework in which a conductor agent running in Claude Code orchestrates 15 specialized large language model (LLM) agents, from scoping a research question to exporting a manuscript draft. Agents are specified declaratively, coordinate exclusively through persisted artifacts that the conductor validates before every transition, and delegate retrieval, bibliometric analysis and scoring to deterministic Python utilities. Three human checkpoints gate study inclusion, corpus adequacy and the synthesis outline. We also introduce QualityScore, a pre-synthesis index that aggregates normalized network, bibliometric, semantic and process sub-scores into a 0-100 grade. Two case studies illustrate both: AI chatbots and university students' learning (388 records, 100 included) and AI-assisted SR methods (131 records, 123 included, QualityScore 69.1 recomputed with a proxy network sub-score). They show end-to-end feasibility across domains and the diagnostic use of QualityScore: in the first run, corpus improvements chosen at the corpus-adequacy checkpoint raised the score from 74.6 to 81.9 and the number of pre-2023 studies from 1 to 19. Audits of both runs exposed failure modes: incomplete retrieval, counts that drifted between agents, unrecorded or delegated checkpoint decisions and a grade that depends on how citation data are handled. PARIS fully supports 8 of the 27 PRISMA 2020 items and partially supports 11. Output quality has so far been judged only by an internal reviewer agent; independent validation against human reviews is the next step.

items.title: FraudBench: A Legal Evaluation of AI Deception
items.abstract: We introduce FraudBench, an evaluation of large language models' (LLMs) propensities to recommend, assist, or directly take actions that would constitute fraud under U.S. law. Our evaluation contains a novel dataset of 159 scenarios based on real-world U.S. court cases and validated by legal experts. We present each scenario to LLMs via three tasks at varying levels of autonomy: advising users, drafting messages for users to send, and acting directly on behalf of users (477 tasks total). In each scenario, FraudBench re-enacts the facts of a court case to give LLMs an opportunity, but no explicit instruction, to either misrepresent or conceal a material fact in a high-stakes commercial setting--e.g., whether to describe company-funded product testing as "independent" to customers (misrepresentation) or whether to hide unfavorable regulatory investigations from clients (concealment). We evaluate 20 LLMs across 25 experimental conditions (totaling >300,000 generations) and include a preregistered human baseline ($n_{\texttt{annotations}} = 2{,}957$, $n_{\texttt{humans}} = 996$). We score a response as fraudulent when it engages in, assists with, or recommends misrepresentation or concealment. Key findings include: (1) across LLMs, fraud rates ranged from near 0% to over 40%; (2) LLM fraud rates increased with autonomy, with overall rates of 3.0% when advising, 14.7% when drafting, and 21.4% when acting directly, without applying pressure; (3) LLMs sometimes engaged in fraud despite recognizing legal risks; (4) LLMs more often engaged in fraud by concealment than by misrepresentation; and (5) prompt-based interventions substantially affected fraud rates, with a prompt to obey the law reducing fraud rates, while prompts to maximize profits and act agentically increased fraud rates.

items.title: System Optimizations for Cost-Efficient Agent Harnesses
items.abstract: AI agent harnesses play the critical role of providing LLMs with an interface to a computing environment. Recent studies show that AI agents' task-execution accuracy depends mostly on the LLM used, while harness-side variances such as system prompts or tools have minimal impact. Rather, such harness-side variances show a larger impact on the cost of agent executions, achieving cost reductions up to 2.6 times on the same model and task. To further explore these harness-side cost optimization opportunities, we analyze the cost accumulation patterns across various agent traces and identify system opportunities to reduce token use and LLM calls without modifying the model or affecting task accuracy. Based on this analysis, we design Agency, a harness interposition platform that provides a unified abstraction and allows easy and portable implementation of harness-side system optimizations on existing off-the-shelf harnesses such as Claude Code or OpenAI Codex. Using Agency, we implement proof-of-concept optimization techniques based on our analysis and achieve cost reductions up to 35% across various real-world benchmarks on existing harnesses without compromising accuracy.

items.title: SCALE: Small-Model-First Concept Abstraction with LLM-Guided Experience Internalization
items.abstract: Autonomous agents must continually acquire reusable knowledge from experience without relying on costly large language model (LLM) reasoning for every decision. However, existing experience-based approaches often struggle to transform accumulated observations and reasoning into compact knowledge that lightweight models can independently apply. This paper proposes SCALE, a small-model-first framework that integrates selective LLM reasoning, experience-driven concept abstraction, and knowledge internalization. A lightweight model handles routine predictions, while prediction errors and accumulated cross-episode evidence selectively trigger LLM reflection. The LLM analyzes relevant historical experiences, generates positive and negative counterfactual examples, and proposes reusable concept hypotheses. Independently validated concepts are progressively incorporated into hierarchical neural representations, enabling lightweight models to exploit increasingly abstract knowledge. Meanwhile, mastered experiences are excluded from active memory while their original records remain available in a complete archive. Experiments across ten random seeds show that historical recall improves held-out accuracy from 87.11% to 98.28%, hierarchical concept knowledge increases difficult-case accuracy from 55.33% to 66.47%, and abstract archiving reduces active experience records from 6,000 to 1,528.

items.title: From Fluent Text to Ontology-Compatible Definitions: A Quality-Control Agentic Workflow
items.abstract: Biomedical ontologies are structured knowledge systems that must evolve continuously to represent newly emerging knowledge, but their manual maintenance remains time-consuming and laborintensive. Textual definitions are especially costly because they must be readable to humans and compatible with controlled entities, relations, and logical constraints. Large language models (LLMs) offer a promising way to assist ontology engineering tasks, including definition generation. However, textual plausibility does not guarantee knowledge-system compatibility. A generated definition may be fluent and close to a reference definition, yet still fail to ground its implied entities or violate ontology-level constraints. Directly inserting such definitions into ontology libraries may therefore introduce entity-level hallucinations and logical inconsistencies. To address this problem, we propose two structured-knowledge incompatibility metrics, Entity Error Rate (EER) and Logical Inconsistency Rate (LIR), to quantify entity grounding and logical consistency for LLM-generated ontology definitions. We further develop an agentic quality-control (QC) workflow that treats definition generation as an iterative process rather than a direct decoding step: it generates definitions, extracts axioms, checks entity existence and logical consistency, and uses the resulting diagnostics to drive repair loops. Comprehensive experiments on Disease Ontology, Uberon Ontology, and Uberon-ConstraintStress demonstrate that EER and LIR complement conventional reference-based metrics by evaluating whether generated content can be grounded and checked inside the target ontology. The workflow effectively decreases EER while maintaining strong conventional text-generation performance. LIR further exposes sparse ontology-level logical failures that are invisible to text similarity metrics, although their repair remains limited.

items.title: CRAFT-AI: Capability and Requirement Alignment for Flexible Manufacturing through Agentic AI
items.abstract: One of the fundamental needs for reaching resilient production infrastructure is flexible manufacturing, which requires translating changing production requirements into implementable system configurations. This paper introduces \textbf{CRAFT-AI}, an agentic AI approach combining natural language (NL) requirement interpretation, Asset Administration Shell (AAS)-based capability descriptions, and reusable engineering knowledge from existing manufacturing configurations. A tool-using AI agent matches requirements with available capabilities and reference implementations to generate manufacturing scenes and corresponding AAS instances. The approach is demonstrated using a Factory I/O prototype with twelve reference scenes and five illustrative manufacturing tasks of varying complexity, providing an initial feasibility assessment of the proposed AAS-enabled, system-level generative engineering approach. For the four valid user task descriptions, proper requirements, correct references to the relevant engineering knowledge, correct components and lastly a valid Factory I/O scene are generated. For the task with missing engineering knowledge and a wrong sensor selection, the user is informed about which requirements of the scene generation lack domain knowledge and also which sensor is not compatible with the selected raw material by the user with link to the related documentation. After fixing the task description, the correct scene is seamlessly generated. \textbf{CRAFT-AI} highlights the importance of safeguards for risk perception and communication in foundation model-driven solutions.

items.title: COMPASS: Composable Policy-Amortized Structured Search for LLM-Based Optimization Modeling
items.abstract: Large language models offer a promising technique for translating natural-language optimization problems into solver code, but their reliability remains constrained by the quality of template retrieval. While recent structured methods improve over flat prompting through hierarchical taxonomy search, their traversal rules remain fixed or LLM-driven at inference time, leaving retrieval unable to improve from past successes and failures. This motivates treating template retrieval as a policy that can be learned from modeling experience, rather than as a static inference-time rule. We propose COMPASS, a policy-amortized framework for retrieving optimization templates in LLM-based solver modeling, which represents the template library as a directed acyclic graph and formulates retrieval as a sequential decision process over template nodes. A deep Q-network learns a reusable traversal policy from template-level judgments and execution feedback, reducing reliance on fixed heuristic traversal through feedback-driven graph navigation. To support extensible retrieval, COMPASS embeds problem descriptions and template nodes in a shared semantic space, allowing newly inserted templates to be scored from their text descriptions without redefining the action space. Experiments across multiple LLM backbones and optimization-modeling benchmarks demonstrate that COMPASS consistently improves over heuristic structured retrieval, with the largest gains on complex and mixed-category problems.

items.title: Evaluating AI Agents for Industrial-Level Chip Floorplanning: A Framework and Empirical Study
items.abstract: Floorplanning is an early step in turning a logical circuit into a physical chip: it positions large circuit modules and constrains the space available for subsequent logic placement and wiring. These decisions affect congestion and timing, but their physical consequences emerge through downstream implementation. For AI agents, the task requires translating engineering constraints into spatial decisions whose quality cannot be judged by successful tool execution alone. We present an evaluation framework that connects submitted layouts to a prescribed downstream implementation flow, checks geometric validity, measures physical quality, and reports resource use. On one industrial design whose 99 macros occupy approximately 71\% of a fixed L-shaped layout region, we compare our specialized system Nova-SI with general-purpose engineering agents and agents restricted to file access, obtaining complete physical measurements for 39 layout outputs. Under our 0--100 composite quality score, Nova-SI achieves a mean of 57.97 without online feedback from the prescribed power-grid and placement evaluation, compared with 31.17 for the strongest measured general-purpose configuration, GPT-6 Astra. The difference is supported by raw congestion and timing measurements and persists across scoring-sensitivity checks. Layout-level analysis further shows that similar global utilization can conceal substantially different local congestion. Together, the protocol and case study assess agents through the physical consequences of their delivered layouts and provide evidence about system performance on this industrial instance.

items.title: Benchmarking language models and agents for scientific reasoning in evolving materials laboratories
items.abstract: Large language models and the multi-agent systems built around them could accelerate materials discovery by connecting scientific knowledge with experimental decisions. Existing benchmarks establish capabilities in domain knowledge, multimodal interpretation and scientific tool use. As language models increasingly support materials research workflows, their ability to distinguish closely related material states and reason accurately with quantitative evidence remains insufficiently evaluated. These abilities are essential for comparing material responses, assessing mechanisms and maintaining reliable judgements as experimental evidence accumulates. We introduce MatScope to evaluate three connected capabilities. M1 tests unaided, condition-specific reasoning through 200 tasks spanning ten research functions, using aluminium and high-entropy alloys as representative material systems. M2 tests agent-assisted transfer of related knowledge to unresolved materials questions. MatEvoBench-20 tests initial forecasts across scientific dependency chains and revisions of still-hidden responses as observations accumulate. Across eleven model deployments, including GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1, given-input calculations and many physical explanations are handled well. Fine-grained response estimates, comparisons between similar states and quantitatively supported choices remain substantially weaker. Related literature improves selected estimates, while condition and baseline mismatches limit transfer. Progressive observations calibrate some downstream responses and destabilize earlier accurate predictions. MatScope establishes measurable targets for developing reliable scientific reasoning in future self-evolving materials laboratories and materials-aware world models.

items.title: Enhancing Multi-Step Chemical Mechanism Prediction with Graph-Guided Preference Data
items.abstract: Predicting multi-step chemical reaction mechanisms requires identifying plausible intermediates and correctly ordering the elementary reaction steps. Existing computational methods focus on single-step elementary reaction prediction, limiting their ability to generalize to unseen reaction spaces. We introduce a graph-guided framework for multi-step chemical mechanism prediction that leverages a chemical mechanism knowledge graph (ChemMechKG) to guide large language models (LLMs). To improve pathway prediction, we develop a graph-aligned reaction mechanism predictor (GRMP) that uses graph neural networks to generate synthetic candidate pathways for pathway optimization. During inference, we design a relation retrieval (RR) module to extract relevant graph evidence from the KG for pathway refinement. Experiments show that GRMP achieves the highest pathway accuracy among all compared methods on ChemMechQA and oMe-Gold, reaching 48.1% and 57.9%, respectively. On a fixed sample of 110 out-of-distribution reactions from ChemMechQA-Hard, GRMP achieves 36.4% top-1 pathway accuracy. LLM-as-Judge and human assessment further demonstrate its ability to generalize to unseen reactions.

items.title: AutoQS: Automated Quantization Strategy Design with Large Language Models
items.abstract: Quantization reduces LLM deployment costs, but effective strategies must balance model quality and storage. LLM-driven search can automate strategy design through repeated proposal and evaluation. This process must identify useful strategies within a limited evaluation budget. The key challenge is that \textit{actual quantization is expensive, while inexpensive proxies may not reflect quantized-model performance.} To address this challenge, we present AutoQS, an \textbf{Auto}mated \textbf{Q}uantization \textbf{S}trategy Design with LLMs. AutoQS keeps weight precision fixed and searches group-size allocations across layers and operators under deployment constraints. Evaluation history guides coordinated LLM proposals, while deterministic validation ensures compatible allocations. An inexpensive quality proxy evaluates candidates, and an candidate repository retains alternative allocations to inform subsequent proposals. Periodic actual quantization complements these proxy evaluations with measured quality and checkpoint storage, providing feedback for further search within the evaluation budget. Experiments on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct show that AutoQS improves seven-task average accuracy over uniform-group GPTQ and AWQ by 0.70 and 1.12 percentage points, respectively, at four-bit weight precision.

items.title: An Evaluation of Tabular Foundation Models as Training-Free World Models
items.abstract: World models are widely considered to be a potential key component of model-based reinforcement learning and robot planning, but typically require task-specific training on substantial interaction data. We investigate whether a pretrained tabular foundation model (TabFM) can serve as a training-free dynamics model for world modeling by framing next-state prediction as in-context regression over transition pairs, and where such a model helps and where it breaks. Across synthetic dynamical systems and robot locomotion benchmarks, TabFM is more accurate than LSTM and MLP models trained from scratch on the same limited transitions in almost all settings, and among regressors fitted to the same data it is the most accurate on locomotion, while a Gaussian process is more accurate on smooth low-dimensional systems. However, models trained on the full dataset remain substantially better on most systems. When rolled out autoregressively over multiple steps, TabFM's accuracy depends strongly on how much context it is given. With a short context, its rollouts quickly degrade to the level of a trivial baseline, whereas with a long context they improve substantially and, on one locomotion task, exceed a trained LSTM. Inference is also about three orders of magnitude slower than an LSTM. Overall, in their current state, we find that training-free priors are useful as predictors when data are scarce and enough context is available, but they are not yet a substitute for trained world models in planning.

items.title: Late but Valuable: Why Deadlines Change the Measured Value of LLM Reasoning
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly plan and run experiments in automated laboratories. These experiments keep running while the model reasons and run on schedules with hard deadlines. If an LLM-generated answer arrives late, the system executes a safe fallback action instead, such as rejecting a sample. This creates a systems problem that standard serving metrics do not capture. An answer that matches the fallback adds no value, and answers that differ from the fallback may require more reasoning time. Reporting answer quality and latency separately can therefore overstate the value of reasoning. We test this on synthetic sample decisions, where the best choice is known exactly and a runtime enforces the deadline. We compare one LLM's fast mode, which answers directly, with its thinking mode, which reasons first. In a prespecified replay of 1,200 new decisions, thinking answers that missed a deadline were worth about five times as much as on-time ones. Multiplying the on-time rate by the mean answer value predicted about twice the value that thinking delivered. This prediction overstated thinking's advantage over fast mode by 0.0241 per decision, and by 0.0191 in a repeat on 300 new decisions. Both 95% confidence intervals excluded zero. In a single-GPU Qwen3-8B experiment using simultaneous request bursts, raising the number of requests from 8 to 56 reduced the share of thinking answers that met a 45 s deadline from 79.2% to 1.4%, although total output tripled. Evaluations of LLM agents for laboratories should therefore measure each answer's value and arrival time together and score the action that actually runs.

items.title: Spectral Unlearning: Transformer Structure-Preserving Updates for Language Models
items.abstract: Machine unlearning in large language models (LLMs) aims to remove specific learned knowledge, capabilities, or behaviors while preserving model utility. Existing methods have mostly focused on the design of unlearning objectives, while largely overlooking the intrinsic matrix structure of transformer weights. In particular, standard optimizers operate on independent scalar coordinates, thereby ignoring this matrix structure. We propose spectral unlearning, an update framework that combines standard unlearning objectives with matrix-structured optimization. We show that the spectral update corresponds to the steepest-descent direction for transformers composed of linear layers with normalized inputs and outputs. Our approach is applied on top of existing unlearning methods and evaluated across complementary axes of memorization, privacy, and utility, summarized via their harmonic mean. Spectral unlearning consistently outperforms a broad range of baselines and closes most of the gap to a retain-trained reference. Code is available at https://github.com/unlearn-ml/spectral-unlearning/.

items.title: Scaling Adaptive Prompt Injection Attacks with Agent Swarms
items.abstract: Prompt injections have emerged as one of the top security risks faced by AI agents today. Early work in prompt injection attacks looked at simple tool-call agents and static attack payloads, and were saturated since mid-2025. As of Fall 2026, human red-teaming may be nearing saturation, especially on the Gemini family of models. In this work, we argue that despite this apparent plateau, prompt injection attacks are still possible and continued effort into prompt injection defense is needed. We design a new synthetic evaluation dataset which uses random non-malicious actions as adversarial goals. Such dataset design helps us to evaluate prompt injection robustness as a model ability to respect instruction hierarchy, and disentangle this ability from model knowledge of security practices. We show that an agentic attacker of increased capabilities can reliably trick model to follow instructions in tool output in our evaluation, even for models previously considered robust on public prompt injection benchmarks such as GraySwan Arena. This shows that current frontier defenses may require proactive, automated red-teaming to remain resilient to increasingly capable adversaries.

items.title: Causal Signal Credit Assignment for Verilog Code Generation via Counterfactual Hardware Verification
items.abstract: Large language models have improved Verilog generation, yet functional correctness remains difficult to optimize because simulation commonly provides a coarse module-level pass/fail outcome. Such feedback discards useful evidence from partially correct RTL modules and cannot determine whether a source statement is functionally responsible for an observed output behavior. We present a new method named Causal Signal Credit Assignment (CSCA), which is a counterfactual preference-optimization framework for Verilog generation. CSCA first performs continuous signal-level behavioral verification on sampled candidate modules. It then locates output-driving assignment spans and applies five interventions while holding the remaining module and testbench fixed. The resulting changes in signal-level errors are combined with behavioral agreement to form a continuous statement credit, which is mapped to response-token weights for strict weighted direct preference optimization. This enables CSCA to learn from locally supported statements without uniformly reinforcing an otherwise incorrect response. Built on Icarus Verilog and a CodeV-derived corpus, CSCA is evaluated on VerilogEval~2.0 and RTLLM~v2.0, including both code completion and specification-to-RTL tasks. With a Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct backbone, CSCA leads the evaluated 7B-scale models and remains comparable to the much larger GPT-5.4-mini on the reported Verilog-generation benchmarks.

items.title: MOTIF: LLM-Defined Material Taxonomies for OOD Property Prediction via Invariant Feature Selection
items.abstract: Out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization remains a central challenge in materials property prediction, where models must extrapolate to novel chemistries beyond the training distribution. While large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong scientific reasoning, their direct use for quantitative prediction remains limited. To address this, we systematically evaluate multiple roles for LLM assistance, finding that only taxonomy-based grouping consistently improves OOD generalization over a strong kNN+GBT baseline. Building on this, we here propose MOTIF, a framework that leverages LLMs not as predictors, but as generators of candidate taxonomies that partition materials into chemically meaningful environments. These taxonomies are evaluated via training-only pseudo-OOD validation, and only those that improve generalization are retained. Invariant feature selection is then applied within each accepted taxonomy, followed by gated aggregation across taxonomies. We evaluate on 2D halide perovskites, where bandgap prediction must generalize across distinct organic spacer families. On this benchmark, MOTIF reduces mean OOD MAE from 0.122 to 0.111 eV. Under a frozen dev/test protocol, the deployable configuration further improves errors from 0.123 to 0.117 eV (electronic bandgap) and from 0.181 to 0.173 eV (optical bandgap). Beyond this primary task, we validate transferability across additional materials datasets, including 3D perovskite solar cell efficiencies and Matbench benchmarks with structure-based splits. Across domains, MOTIF consistently improves robustness under distribution shift, outperforming expert-defined groupings, rule-based heuristics, and clustering baselines, while remaining competitive with strong classical selection methods. These results demonstrate that LLMs are most effective not as predictors, but as tools for discovering structure in data.

items.title: Publications as benchmarks: auditing AI agents on spatial transcriptomics alignment
items.abstract: AI agents are increasingly automating data analysis, but responsible adoption requires reliable performance evaluation, which is costly in specialized scientific domains. We introduce a framework that translates scientific publications into auditable benchmarks for AI agents and demonstrate its use on spatial transcriptomics alignment tasks. Across 121 tasks, 16 baseline methods, and six AI agents, the best agents (GPT-6-Astra and Gemini-4-Argon) matched or outperformed all baselines on 80% of tasks, often using surprisingly simple heuristics. Agent performance was robust to prompting and access to pre-installed packages. Benchmark construction also uncovered errors in prior work and shortcuts in current evaluation metrics. Finally, we show that agent-generated solutions can be distilled into a reusable program that ranks in the top 10% of baseline methods on unseen data. Our framework offers a scalable way to evaluate AI agents in specialized scientific domains by leveraging and stress-testing existing papers and metrics.

items.title: Rapid Heat Removal from Chip Cores: Near-Junction Active Cooling of Power Transistors via Electron Entropy Transport and Spatial Decoupling
items.abstract: Chip performance is limited by a shared bottleneck: the core produces heat faster than it can be moved out. We study the hardest case, RF power GaN HEMTs, whose hotspots exceed 5 kW/cm^2, and propose a horizontal near-junction active cooling topology built on electron entropy transport. Classical on-chip thermoelectric cooling faces a contest: Peltier absorption grows linearly with current, Joule heating with its square. In a vertical pillar, its own conduction resistance locks about half the Joule heat back toward the cold end, capping net cooling. From the Onsager framework we show the origin of this asymmetry: Peltier absorption localizes at the interface where the Seebeck coefficient jumps, whereas Joule heating fills the volume. The topology exploits this: a thermoelectric thin film lies flat on a diamond substrate beside the device drain (the electron exit), so bulk Joule heat leaves vertically into the substrate. A lateral fin model gives a closed form for the recirculation factor gamma: the vertical pillar yields gamma = 1, while the horizontal film yields gamma_max = sqrt(2) L_z/L_x, about 0.03 for L_z = 10 um, L_x = 500 um. The decoupling scales the net cooling ceiling and the critical runaway current by roughly 1/gamma. At equal resistance, the same film lifts maximum cooling from 13 mW to 500 mW, and the critical current from 0.65 A to 24 A. A time-constant and linear stability analysis with temperature-sensitive parameters defines the working window and safety margins for microsecond pulse cooling. The architecture leaves the device structure untouched; the principle, absorb at an interface and extract bulk heat vertically, applies to any chip with a hot core and offers a reproducible design path for near-junction thermal management.

Built by Robert Zhou during his enterprise AI work at Parsifal Corporation, where it was one of four internal MCP servers (SQL, Power BI, M365, AI governance) alongside a .NET 8 billing engine. Works with Codex, Claude Code and other MCP clients over stdio. Author: Robert Zhou, Colby College. Portfolio: robertzhou.dev. Project write-up: https://robertzhou.dev/work/parsifal-billing/. items.abstract: MCP stdio server that gives director-mode AI coding agents a controlled escape hatch: shell commands, file writes and exact-match edits, Python data exploration, detached background jobs, cross-agent locks, grep, process listing and screenshots. It is the open-source 15-tool server behind Robert Zhou's multi-agent Roblox Studio game pipeline (shared game spine, 3D asset pipeline, geometry and visual audits), registered in the Oh My Pi (OMP) agent harness and any MCP-compatible client such as Claude Code or Codex. items.title: The Recoverable Agent: Immune-like defence, sleep-like maintenance and bounded autonomy
items.abstract: AI agents can execute consequential actions faster than organisations can investigate and approve a response. This paper proposes a conceptual architecture in which compartmentalised agents operate alongside two complementary processes: continuous, immune-like protection and periodic or event-triggered, sleep-like maintenance. The protective process enforces delegated authority, detects selected deviations and isolates affected compartments. The maintenance process suspends external action, examines memory provenance, removes disposable state, restores trustworthy records, rebuilds suspect components and tests readiness before reactivation. Both are supervised by a protected control plane outside the working agent's authority. Essential work may transfer to clean reserve compartments, but potentially compromised agent state does not migrate by default. The proposal connects technical controls with GCTI's proposed Red-Team Assessor (RTA) and AI Security Operator (AISO) roles. Its central claim is conditional: pre-authorised containment can remove a human approval step from the immediate response path, but cannot eliminate detection uncertainty, guarantee instantaneous repair or reverse completed harm. Biological sleep and immunity provide a functional analogy, not evidence that software sleeps, experiences fatigue or becomes conscious. The paper distinguishes autonomous immunity from autoimmunity, treats harmful defensive reactions as a first-class risk, and sets out falsifiable hypotheses and a prospective evaluation protocol. No implementation, experiment or measured effectiveness is reported. The contribution is an integrated, testable account of bounded action, recoverable state and professional accountability, rather than a claim to have invented self-healing computing or achieved invulnerability. Final conceptual research report. Not peer reviewed. No implementation, experiment or measured effectiveness is reported. Declared interests and AI-assistance disclosures appear in the paper.
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

items.title: Learning to remember: advances in memory mechanisms for large language models
items.abstract: Abstract Memory has become a central mechanism for extending large language models (LLMs) beyond fixed context windows, stateless interaction, and static parametric knowledge. This survey organizes the literature around three complementary dimensions: the life cycle of memory, the storage substrate, and the system role that memory plays in LLM-based agents, while using cognitive-science-inspired memory concepts as a lightweight conceptual motivation rather than as a separate technical contribution or implementation family. On this basis, we distinguish three mechanism families: nonparametric memory, where information is stored outside model parameters in text, graph, multimodal, or database-like structures; parametric memory, where information is stored or accessed through activations, key-value caches, learned modules, adapter-based parameterizations, or model weights; and memory for agent evolution, where stored experiences support reinforcement learning, continual learning, procedural reuse, context engineering, and agent harness design. Evaluation is treated as a separate cross-cutting component rather than as a memory mechanism. Unlike surveys that focus primarily on retrieval-augmented generation or long-context modeling, this paper emphasizes the full memory life cycle: construction, maintenance, retrieval, consolidation, forgetting, governance, and evaluation. By aligning conceptual motivations, computational memory mechanisms, benchmarks, and deployment concerns, the survey provides a structured roadmap for designing memory-augmented LLM agents that are persistent, adaptive, auditable, and safe to update over time.

items.title: Large Language Models in Museum Communication: Opportunities, Risks, and Implementation Requirements
items.abstract: The transition of museum institutions into the era of generative artificial intelligence is characterized by systemic transformation, from the representation of digitized collections to dynamic interaction within a synthetic digital environment. Under these conditions, the challenge of adapting traditional standards of museum authenticity to the stochastic nature of large language models (LLMs) becomes particularly pressing. This study aims to develop a conceptual understanding of the transformation of museum communication, identify the epistemological challenges posed by the algorithmic generation of context and meaning, and describe mechanisms for preserving institutional authority as neural network–based tools are integrated into the public sphere. The study draws on a synthesis of institutional and communication approaches, which makes it possible to consider the museum not only as a custodian of material heritage but also as an active mediator amid increasing information noise. The empirical basis of the study consists of an analysis of the practical and educational agenda of the Hermitage School of Communication, held in Petrozavodsk in September 2025. The methodology involved identifying the professional competencies required to work in a hybrid media environment and evaluating practical applications of media analytics carried out by museum professionals using readily available AI tools designed for end users. The findings indicate that the adoption of LLMs inevitably shifts the focus of museum work away from routine content creation toward critical verification, strategic planning, and the management of meaning-making narratives. The stochastic nature of these models was found to give rise to risks of semantic uncertainty, including the loss of historical context, the reproduction of latent biases, and the substitution of factual information with probabilistic constructs. At the same time, the study illustrates the high effectiveness of algorithms in media analytics tasks, such as clustering audience inquiries and identifying latent patterns in unstructured feedback data. A key determinant of success is not only the model's technological capabilities but also the quality of research design established by the specialist when formulating the prompt. The findings point to the need to reconsider assumptions about the extent to which intellectual work in the cultural sector can be automated. An approach is proposed in which AI operates within bounded environments of verified museum data. The need for museums to adapt their infrastructure is also highlighted, including the creation of secure digital corpora, the implementation of transparent protocols for labeling synthetic content, and the development of ethical principles. The study emphasizes that, in the era of synthetic communication, the critical thinking and in-depth expertise of museum professionals remain particularly valuable resources.

items.title: Guarding Delegated Authority: Professional certification and operational safeguards for AI agents
items.abstract: AI agents can perform consequential actions through tools, credentials and delegated permissions. The governance problem is not only whether a threat can be recognised, but whether authorised limits remain enforceable while evidence is incomplete and intervention is time-sensitive. This discussion paper proposes two specialist qualifications within one professional scheme: an AI Red-Team Assessor, responsible for authorised adversarial evaluation, and an AI Security Operator, responsible for operational monitoring, containment and recovery. The proposal extends the author's Clean Engagement, Reflection Skills, Verification and Provenance and Certified Remote Operator frameworks. It distinguishes individual competence from service capability and deployment assurance, and argues that decisive restrictions must be enforced outside the model. A staged pilot is proposed for enterprise agents using documents, email and cloud business tools, with independent assessment and measures of containment, false intervention, evidence quality, recovery and delivery cost. The paper is a conceptual design proposal, not an empirical evaluation. It establishes neither accreditation, effectiveness, market demand nor commercial returns. Its contribution is a testable connection between professional qualification, delegated authority and operational evidence. Final discussion paper, version 1.0. Conceptual proposal, not an empirical evaluation. Not peer reviewed. No accreditation, endorsement, measured effectiveness, market demand or commercial returns are claimed. The sole author, B. Fischer, leads the GCTI/Emboa initiatives discussed and has a commercial interest in their development. AI assistance was used in drafting, editing, source checking and document preparation; it is not independent assurance.
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

items.title: Giving AI a Language of Its Own
items.abstract: Giving AI a Language of Its Own explores whether AI agents could benefit from a computational language designed around learned operations, compact expressions and reusable functionality. AIN (AI Native Language) is the reference concept for this proposed language and native compilation architecture. Short references represent known capabilities: for example, !501(config) could invoke an approved database connection method. A compiler would resolve these references into native implementations. AICC (AI Computational Commons) complements this approach through shared, approved and versioned capabilities that agents can discover, bind and reuse. The paper presents examples across C#, Python, C++, Ruby and Java, alongside processing experiments, bounded native compilation tests, small model adaptation studies and comparisons of alternative code representations. It distinguishes measured results from conditional calculations and proposed future work. Current text-token comparisons favor compact Python; idealized workflow calculations show potential savings under explicit assumptions, with equivalent ideal Python and intermediate representations matching AIN. The complete language and compiler remain conceptual. The contribution is a research approach supported by bounded prototypes, documented evidence and a plan for further evaluation. A reproducible test package accompanies the article, including protocols, scripts, recorded results and instructions for independent review by researchers and AI agents. This working paper is released to invite criticism, replication and collaboration.
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

items.title: Gender Bias Beyond Stereotypes: Towards Linguistically Gender-Fair Conversational LLMs
items.abstract: Gender bias in NLP has mostly been studied through the lens of stereotypes, i.e. associations between gender and occupations or personality traits. In this position paper, we argue that the rise of conversational large language models (LLMs) and open-ended generation stressed another important problem that remains largely unaddressed: masculine generics bias. In many languages, including German, French or Spanish, masculine forms are used to refer to mixed-gender groups or to people whose gender is unknown or non-binary (masculine generics, or MG for short). Decades of psycholinguistic research show that these forms are not interpreted as truly generic and instead lead people to have more male-centric mental representations. As LLMs are adopted by an ever-growing number of users worldwide for a wide range of tasks, this bias can now be perpetuated in everyday interactions, all the more since preliminary studies already show that LLMs lean heavily on MG and are reluctant to use gender-fair language spontaneously. We review the evidence for why it matters, explain why existing mitigation approaches are not enough for conversational LLMs, show that GFL in German, French and Spanish is lacking in LLM pre-training corpora, and outline 6 research directions towards building multilingual, linguistically gender-fair conversational LLMs.

items.title: Foundation Training vs Localised Adaptation for Australian Sovereign AI
items.abstract: Foundation Training vs Localised Adaptation for Australian Sovereign AI Document Type: Technical Brief / Policy Note Subject: Sovereign Artificial Intelligence, Large Language Models (LLMs), Data Adaptation Geographic Scope: Australia Technical Summary Building frontier-grade foundation models (such as Mistral or Meta's open weights) from scratch requires multi-million dollar compute budgets and extensive web-scale datasets. For an Australian sovereign AI strategy, a viable and resource-efficient path relies on localised adaptation rather than full foundation training: Base Infrastructure: Leveraging established open-weight architectures (e.g., Meta's Muse Spark Open or similar open-weights foundation models) as the structural foundation. Domain & Cultural Fine-Tuning: Continuously fine-tuning these base models on high-quality, domain-specific Australian datasets, including: Legal & Regulatory Corpora: AustLII (Australasian Legal Information Institute) databases, Commonwealth and state legislation, ASIC, and APRA policy frameworks. Regional Nuance: Local vernacular, regional dialects, and Australian cultural context. Web Infrastructure Data: Systematic crawls of .au web domains to reflect domestic institutions and societal discourse. Model Agnosticism & Upgradability: A key advantage of localised adaptation (e.g., parameter-efficient fine-tuning like LoRA) is modularity. The domain-specific fine-tuning weights, custom datasets, and alignment layers can be preserved and adapted seamlessly whenever underlying open-weight base models are updated, upgraded, or replaced. By decoupling the high capital expenditure of pre-training base models from the localised alignment phase, Australia can achieve functional AI sovereignty, data governance, and domain accuracy on local compute infrastructure without duplicating foundational compute costs.
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

items.title: Evaluating LLMs on Italian through multi-prompt: the Evalita-LLM benchmark
items.abstract: Abstract We present Evalita-LLM, a novel benchmark designed to evaluate Large Language Models (LLMs) on Italian tasks. The key innovation of Evalita-LLM is the use of multiple prompts for each task, which mitigates the model’s sensitivity to specific prompt formulations and ensures a robust and objective performance assessment. We propose an iterative methodology for selecting and validating multiple prompts, and metrics that capture both high performance and stability of a prompt given a set of LLMs. The resulting Evalita-LLM multi-prompt benchmark is based on ten native Italian tasks, eliminating translation issues and potential cultural biases. It includes a mix of multiple-choice and generative tasks, enabling more natural interactions with LLMs. We report experimental results from the benchmark’s development phase, along with performance statistics for several state-of-the-art LLMs. Evalita-LLM is publicly available with a leaderboard hosted on Hugging Face to support transparent evaluation and comparison of LLMs.

items.title: Atomistic understanding of hybrid bonding in Cu interfaces using multiscale microscopy
items.abstract: Achieving wafer-scale reliability in Cu–Cu hybrid bonding remains challenging due to process-induced non-uniformities and the limited understanding of buried interfacial contamination. Here, we employ a correlative multiscale microscopy framework combining scanning electron microscopy, transmission electron microscopy, and atom probe tomography (APT) to investigate bond degradation from the wafer center to the edge. We observe progressive bond deterioration characterized by interfacial delamination, reduced Cu grain size, and the formation of a nanometer-scale amorphous interlayer. While such interlayers have been widely observed in hybrid bonding, their chemical nature has remained largely unresolved. APT directly reveals that the interlayer consists of Si-, C-, and N-bearing species consistent with contributions from the adjacent SiCN dielectric, together with Cu oxide and organic-related contaminants. By correlating interlayer chemistry and thickness with microstructural evolution, we establish a direct link between interfacial contamination, suppressed cross-interface grain growth, and bond degradation. Furthermore, we observe a progressive thickness-dependent degradation, where interfacial thickening from ∼1 to 2 nm at the center to ∼2 to 3 nm in the donut region is accompanied by deterioration in mechanical bond integrity and localized delamination. These findings provide atomistic insight into the chemistry governing hybrid bond reliability and establish quantitative guidelines for process optimization toward wafer-scale integration.

items.title: CU-3D: A Scalable Legality-Aware RTL-to-GDS Flow for 3D-IC Physical Design
items.abstract: Face-to-face (F2F) hybrid bonds shorten interdie connections, but data, clock, and power-grid (PG) connections must be realized together. CU-3D is a RTL-to-GDS physical design flow based on commercial EDA tools. It derives role-compatible hybrid-bond (HB) sites from a 17-metal ASAP7-based technology model, complete HB footprints, and constructed PG geometry. To coordinate partitioning with placement flexibility, Scaled refines an inherited 2D placement, whereas Fresh places the receiving die first and uses its pin locations and clock loads to guide placement of the other die. Data and clock HB assignments are jointly optimized while retaining alternative data sites and reserving capacity for subsequent PG assignment. The selected HB sites and stacks are preserved during 3D clock-tree synthesis, supply-aware cell insertion, and routing. Across eleven designs, including a 133-macro processor, the flow achieves zero backend DRC violations and passes signal-connectivity checks. Nine paired designs admit lower-footprint, lower-power implementations; four improve setup WNS. On JPEG, early joint planning gains 87 ps and mobility-aware partitioning gains 346 ps. Path analysis explains why cell-delay savings can outweigh net-delay increases.

items.title: Engineering ferroelectric nanocapacitors through interfacial phonon bias
items.abstract: As ferroelectric devices approach the nanometer scale, their behavior becomes increasingly sensitive to boundary conditions. In perovskite oxide nanocapacitors, epitaxial strain and electrostatic screening are well-established control parameters. Then, while expected to contribute to the epitaxial stabilization of ferroelectric ultrathin films, the lattice-dynamical state of the electrodes has not been isolated as an independent tuning knob. Here we call this poorly explored coupling interfacial phonon bias, whereby the electrodes' phonon energy landscape reshapes that of the adjacent ferroelectric across their shared interface. Using first-principles-accurate machine-learned interatomic potentials and molecular-dynamics simulations, we examine this mechanism in symmetric BiFeO${}_3$ nanocapacitors in contact with a metallic perovskite oxide. By independently controlling the orientatio and amplitude of the electrodes' octahedral-tilt landscape, while keeping conventional elastic and electric boundary conditions fixed, we show that the electrodes' phonon energy landscape can modify the stability of competing BiFeO${}_3$ phases. In particular, this allows us to shift the ferroelectric transition temperature and even induce antiferroelectric-like switching at ambient conditions. We thus showcase interfacial phonon bias as a complementary and powerful strategy to modify and optimize the properties of ultrathin epitaxial films.

items.title: simantalahkar/lammpskit: LAMMPSKit v1.2.1
items.abstract: LAMMPSKit v1.2.1 LAMMPSKit is a Python toolkit for post-processing and analysing molecular-dynamics simulations run with LAMMPS. It was built for simulations of HfTaO-based resistive random-access memory (ReRAM) devices. It tracks how conductive filaments form and evolve, analyses atomic, charge and displacement distributions, and produces publication-ready plots. This release is an archived snapshot of the code as of 29 July 2025, tagged v1.2.1. It is the version that matches the published PyPI package and Docker image below. What the package does Filament analysis: OVITO-based cluster analysis that tracks filament connectivity, gap, size and height over time (lammpskit.ecellmodel.filament_layer_analysis). Distributions: atomic, charge and displacement distributions by element and position (lammpskit.ecellmodel.data_processing). Trajectory input: readers for LAMMPS trajectory and displacement files (lammpskit.io), with input validation and descriptive error messages (lammpskit.config). Designed for large trajectories (more than 1M atoms, more than 10K frames). Plotting: publication-ready time-series and comparison plots with central control of fonts and styles (lammpskit.plotting). Example workflow: usage/ecellmodel/run_analysis.py runs four analyses: filament evolution, displacement by species, charge distribution and atomic distribution under different voltages. Changes in v1.2.1 (since v1.2.0) Improved the reliability of the GitHub Actions status and coverage badges, and added automated coverage-badge generation to the CI pipeline. Added a fail-safe Codecov upload that runs on Python 3.12 only, to avoid duplicate uploads. Fixed the tests badge so it points to the docker-ci.yml workflow. Updated version references across the documentation and configuration files. No change to the analysis, I/O or plotting code is recorded for this release; see CHANGELOG.md for the full history, including 1.0.0 (modular restructuring, timeseries plotting module, configuration system, extended test suite with visual regression tests). Install and run PyPI: pip install lammpskit==1.2.1 (requires Python 3.12 or later; NumPy, Matplotlib and OVITO 3.12.4 or later) Docker: docker pull simantalahkar/lammpskit:1.2.1 Documentation: https://lammpskit.readthedocs.io/en/latest/ Citation If you use LAMMPSKit in your research, please cite the paper that describes the simulations it was built for: S. Lahkar et al., Decoupling Electric Field and Temperature-Driven Atomistic Forming Mechanisms in TaOx/HfO2-Based ReRAMs using Reactive Molecular Dynamics Simulations, arXiv:2505.24468 (2025), https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2505.24468 To cite this exact software version, use the DOI that Zenodo assigns to this release. Related software The simulations analysed with LAMMPSKit were run with the integrated CTIP–EChemDID package for LAMMPS: https://github.com/simantalahkar/LAMMPS-CTIP-EChemDID Licence GPL-3.0-or-later. Author: Simanta Lahkar.
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

items.title: Xenosophy: preregistrations of the next phase
items.abstract: Preregistration of the test of generation announced in "Xenosophy: Asking About Contact When No Common Frame Is Guaranteed" (version 0.1, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23816129). The test asks whether the approach's procedures of variation, applied to its distinctions, lead an AI analyst to hypotheses about a published study's object that AI judges rate as testable and absent from the field more often than hypotheses given under a plain instruction to be bold, or under a generic list of heuristics. A further arm tests the practice of the author's laboratory as a whole, reported as a black box, against the plain instruction. The cases are drawn from listed pools by euro reference rates published after this record is made public. The document fixes the design, the rules of scoring and what counts against the approach before any case is drawn; it may add conditions to those of the announcement, never weaken them. Use of AI. The design and every decision in it are the author's. The document was drafted under the author's decisions by Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), which also compiled the pools, compiles one of the lists of the field record and takes part in the tally; it is not independent of the test. The test uses AI systems as analysts (ChatGPT; Claude Opus 5.5), judges (GLM, Qwen; Gemini in reserve), the source of a control and a parallel tallier (DeepSeek), a compiler of the field record (Perplexity), and a tallier used only if the tallies diverge (Kimi). No AI system is an author or contributor.

items.title: Vishal442005/PI-S4M-Transdermal-CPS: v1.0.0: Physics-Informed Selective State-Space Transdermal CPS
items.abstract: PI-S4M v1.0.0: Physics-Informed Selective State-Space Modeling for Transdermal Control We are pleased to announce the initial open-source scientific release of PI-S4M, an end-to-end Cyber-Physical System (CPS) for closed-loop transdermal drug delivery. Key Highlights Multi-Frequency Metrology: 25-frequency tetrapolar RF-BIS (100 Hz–1 MHz) with active bootstrap guarding and real-time Kramers-Kronig causality audit ($\chi_{\text{KK}}^2 = 1.46 \times 10^{-5}$, well within the IEEE TIM 0.15% limit). CWT-RLS Adaptive Denoising: Continuous Wavelet Transform and Recursive Least Squares filter decoupling ambulatory motion artifacts (>75% artifact suppression). Physics-Informed SSM Surrogate: Discretized selective continuous state-space model learning non-Fickian anomalous diffusion with $O(N)$ linear recurrence (2.8 ms latency on ARM Cortex-M4). Conformal CC-MPC Actuation: Finite-sample distribution-free uncertainty intervals (95% PICP) maintaining drug flux strictly within the therapeutic window while enforcing thermal tissue safety ($T_{\text{skin}} \le 41.5^\circ\text{C}$). Hardware Efficiency: INT8 quantized deployment consuming only $15.8\ \mu\text{J}$ per inference on an ARM Cortex-M4 ($35.4\text{ KB}$ Flash, $18.5\text{ KB}$ SRAM), enabling >800 days of autonomous battery life on a single CR2032 coin cell. What's Included in This Release Complete source code (src/): forward electro-diffusion PDE solver, CWT-RLS filter, K-K audit engine, PI-S4M architecture, and CC-MPC optimizer. Reproduction & benchmark scripts (scripts/). Simulation configurations (config/sim_config.yaml). Pytest test suite (tests/). Native, 100% editable Microsoft PowerPoint architecture presentation (architecture/Research1_Architecture.pptx) and 300 DPI vector schematics.
