In this paper, we propose TNAS-ER, the first neural architecture search (NAS) framework tailored to TTFS SNNs for eye-based emotion recognition. TNAS-ER presents a novel ANN-assisted search strategy that leverages a ReLU-based ANN counterpart to guide architecture optimization and stabilize training of the TTFS SNN. TNAS-ER employs an evolutionary algorithm, with weighted and unweighted average recall jointly defined as fitness objectives for emotion recognition. Extensive experiments demonstrate that TNAS-ER achieves high recognition performance with significantly improved efficiency. Furthermore, we evaluate TNAS-ER on neuromorphic hardware, confirming its superior energy efficiency and strong potential for real-world applications.
items.venue: ACM International Conference on Multimedia (ACM MM)

items.title: Mid-IR diffraction gratings fabricated via nanoimprint lithography for chirped pulse amplification
items.abstract: Abstract Lasers emitting in the 2 µm spectral region have attracted considerable attention in recent years owing to their wide-ranging applications in science and industry, including the detection of atmospheric constituents like H 2 O, surgical procedures in medicine, and LIDAR technologies. In industry, they can be utilized in high-precision machining and materials engineering. For these latter purposes, a high-power laser is needed. This can be achieved by amplifying the laser pulse, typically using chirped pulse amplification (CPA). The crucial component of CPA, used for the compression and stretching steps, is the grating waveguide structure (GWS). In the present paper, we explore the fabrication of GWSs via nanoimprint lithography (NIL) for operation at a central wavelength of 2050 nm. The GWSs were integrated into the topmost hafnium oxide (HfO₂) layer of a multilayer HfO₂/SiO₂ dielectric mirror. The fabrication process comprised master wafer production via laser interference lithography, stamp fabrication, NIL patterning, and reactive-ion etching. The desired etch depth in HfO 2 was a key challenge, which was addressed by implementing a chromium hard mask and a Taguchi experimental design. Scanning electron microscopy and atomic force microscopy revealed slight deviations from the designed GWS dimensions, mainly in the duty cycle. Consequently, the maximum diffraction efficiency was slightly blue-shifted and measured to be 97% at 2030 nm, i.e., lower than the 99% predicted theoretically. Our study demonstrates the feasibility of using NIL for large-area GWS fabrication with high diffraction efficiency.

items.title: Metrology-Driven Sample Preparation for Advanced Microelectronics Using TESCAN FemtoChisel with Intelligent Multigas Processing, LPL, and AI-Enabled Correlative Workflows
items.abstract: Advanced microelectronics metrology increasingly depends on how the sample is prepared before inspection. In heterogeneous packages, the region of interest may be buried beneath combinations of mold compound, silicon, copper, redistribution layers, dielectrics, underfill, and organic substrate materials. The measurement challenge is therefore not only one of imaging resolution, but also one of physical access: the sample must be opened to the correct level, the exposed structures must remain interpretable, and the preparation geometry must provide useful views of internal layers and interfaces. This paper presents a metrology-driven sample-preparation workflow using the TESCAN FemtoChisel ultrashort-pulsed laser platform. The workflow combines femtosecond laser machining, intelligent multigas processing, laser protective layer strategies, imaging feedback, and AI-enabled process development. The broader platform capability includes controlled package opening, layer exposure, access-window creation, cross-section preparation, and correlative workflows with optical, confocal, SEM/FIB, and X-ray imaging. In this paper, the experimental results focus specifically on demonstrations relevant to metrology access: controlled laser delayering. Specifically, it is shown that the laser process can expose selected package levels and provide intermediate inspection states. Through creation of inverted pyramid structures we demonstrate the ability to stop at the layer of interest. The results support a preparation-to-measurement framework in which laser machining is used not simply to remove material, but to create measurement-ready sample states. Intelligent multigas processing and protective-layer concepts expand the usable process window by improving debris management and boundary preservation. AI-enabled process development and correlative navigation provide a path toward more repeatable and target-aware preparation. Together, these elements position FemtoChisel as a platform for creating controlled access geometries that support advanced package metrology, failure analysis, and process development.

items.title: Memory Fit: Architectural Support for Page Placement by Learning Models of Good Behavior
items.abstract: Server main memory is increasingly heterogeneous, incorporating technologies such as zswap, CXL memory expanders, and emerging phase-change memories (PCM). To decide where to place pages, operating systems have to choose between efficient but coarse-grained access bits, out-of-band profiling, or costly runtime instrumentation. This paper proposes memory fit, a hardware abstraction that provides precise and accurate page placement information to an operating system. Memory fit measures how well a page "fits" each type of memory in the system. Memory fit separates the mechanism of measuring affinity between pages and memories from the OS policy of choosing which pages to move when. The paper describes soft trace matching (STM), a computationally and space efficient algorithm to compute memory fit. The key technical insight behind STM is that it can estimate memory fit by comparing accesses to a page with a learned model of "good" traces for a memory. We have implemented memory fit and STM in a BOOMv3 RISC-V processor running Linux 6.6. On extended GUPS, memory fit placements recover 2.2-3.8 times as much of the performance gap to optimal placement as Linux TPP. For Redis with equal DRAM and PCM capacities, placements selected by memory fit recover 80% of the performance gap, versus 19% for TPP, in a placement replay. Memory fit requires only 64 bits of state per 4 KiB page and can be updated on every main-memory access with only a 1.2% overhead of OS kernel notification processing.

items.title: Low Thermal Damage Laser Lift-off (LLO) Enabling Multi-Cycle Carrier Wafers Reuse for Advanced Packaging
items.abstract: Fusion and hybrid bonding are becoming critical enablers in advanced packaging for die-to-wafer (D2W), high-bandwidth memory (HBM), and artificial intelligence (AI) applications. Laser lift-off (LLO) employing short-pulsed IR laser beam provides a clean and efficient method to release permanently bonded Si carrier wafers without need of a glue layer or backside grinding processes. LLO enables multiple carrier wafer reuse cycles, offering significant cost reduction and environmental sustainability benefits. However, LLO may generate the thermal and mechanical stresses during LLO to impact device integrity. This study investigates thermal damage mechanisms and mitigation strategies for stacked structures during carrier wafer release. Metal silicide phase transitions were characterized by X-ray diffraction (XRD) to detect thermal exposure 200–500 °C, while tracer ion diffusion analysis via time-of-flight secondary ion mass spectrometry (ToF-SIMS) identified thermal exposures in the 800–1000 °C range. These results were calibrated against 60-second rapid thermal annealing (RTA) references to establish a thermal budget for LLO induced energy exposure. The results of these thermal damage experiments were used to model a broader spectrum of stacked materials. The absorption through the stack and the resulting heat transfer were simulated. Since experimental measurements generally require orders of magnitude for longer timescales than laser exposure, it is challenging to compare the energy spike in LLO simulation to a thermal budget based on RTA processing. If for a given stack it has been demonstrated experimentally that the heat energy from the laser is at an acceptable level, then it is reasonable to assume that other stacks that show equal or less heat energy in simulation are also acceptable. This integrated experimental–simulation framework supports optimized stack engineering, ensuring device integrity and sustainable multi-cycle carrier wafer reuse for advanced packaging.

items.title: Ionomer‐Free Iridium Anodes With Low Loading for Zero‐Gap Electrolyzers via Direct Atomic Layer Deposition
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Proton exchange membrane water electrolysis (PEMWE) is among the most promising techniques to provide hydrogen as both energy carrier and feedstock for the chemical industry, due to its compatibility with intermittent renewable electricity sources. However, a major bottleneck in scaling up PEMWE is the limited supply of the anode catalyst Ir. This work shows a novel approach to tailoring ionomer‐free catalyst layers based on custom‐made microporous substrates and two different atomic layer deposition (ALD) processes, both using Ir(EtCp)(CHD) precursor. Thermal ALD using as counter‐reactant yields mostly metallic Ir/ and an electrode Ir loading of 0.21 . The PEMWE cell‐level performance is comparable to a commercial catalyst‐coated membrane anode despite lower loading, and is maintained over an accelerated durability test equivalent to 600 h of intermittent operation. Moreover, using a low‐loading ALD‐made cathode, the total platinum group metal loading is only 0.24 . Plasma‐enhanced ALD reduces the Ir loading to 0.04 by tailoring the catalyst distribution, however, yields lower‐activity . Finally, direct ALD catalyst deposition needs no ionomer‐bearing ink. The anodes are therefore compatible with various membrane materials, as demonstrated in a electrolysis experiment with an anion exchange membrane.

items.title: INSIGHT-X: Multimodal VLM Assistant for Artifact Localization, and Mitigation Guidance in X-ray Inspection
items.abstract: Advanced semiconductor packages rely on X-ray CT and laminography for non-destructive inspection of buried interconnects and internal structures. However, dense metal features and heterogeneous materials often introduce artifacts, including ring artifacts, beam-hardening streaks, geometric distortions, and missing-cone artifacts. These artifacts obscure critical features during inspection, reduce reconstruction fidelity, and complicate defect interpretation, requiring expert-driven and iterative troubleshooting. To address these challenges, we propose INSIGHT-X, a vision–language model framework for artifact diagnosis, localization, root-cause and mitigation in X-ray inspection workflows. INSIGHT-X formulates artifact analysis as a multimodal question-answering task by integrating reconstructed X-ray images, artifact annotations, and expert knowledge into an artifact-centric dataset. Through parameter-efficient fine-tuning, the model learns to identify artifact types, localize affected regions, and generate interpretable explanations. The system also provides artifact-aware cause and mitigation recommendations, including general acquisition and reconstruction adjustments, and calibration guidance. By combining visual understanding, spatial localization with explainable answers, INSIGHT-X transforms expert knowledge into a scalable AI assistant for improving inspection consistency, accelerating troubleshooting, and supporting decision-making in advanced semiconductor manufacturing.

items.title: High-Entropy Design of Commensurate Antiferroelectric Ceramics with Superior Energy Storage Performance
items.abstract: Antiferroelectric (AFE) ceramic dielectrics are imperative for next-generation energy-storage capacitors because of near-zero remnant polarization. In this work, we construct a new high-entropy antiferroelectric ceramic to synergistically optimize dielectric energy storage by reconstructing the commensurate polarization modulation, thereby delivering an ultrahigh recoverable energy density (Wrec) of ∼14.2 J/cm3 at 71 kV/mm while maintaining a high energy efficiency (η) of ∼84%. In addition, the ceramics deliver remarkable fatigue resistance with stable performance over 105 charge-discharge cycles. This study highlights entropy engineering as a powerful framework for designing high-performance AFE energy-storage ceramics and offers insights for the future development of advanced dielectric capacitors.

items.title: Future Directions and Emerging Trends in Food Nanotechnology
items.abstract: Nanotechnology involves controlling and structuring matter at the atomic or molecular level, typically on scales smaller than 100 nm, to develop materials and devices with novel characteristics. It has made significant inroads across various sectors, offering unique applications due to the distinct physical and chemical properties of nanostructured materials. Food nanotechnology has revolutionized the preservation, processing, testing, and packaging of food products. Advanced packaging solutions incorporating nanomaterials have improved the safety, quality, and shelf life of food by maintaining its mechanical and chemical properties while preventing contamination. Various forms of nano-packaging have been developed, including enhanced, active, bio-based, and smart/intelligent packaging. Smart packaging incorporates nanosensors into food packaging, which will likely become more widespread, allowing for real-time monitoring of food safety parameters such as contamination, gas levels, moisture, and temperature. Meanwhile, bio-based packaging is becoming increasingly popular and offers a promising alternative to conventional plastic packaging. However, it still requires further research to overcome challenges related to cost and material properties. Recent advancements in nanotechnology have also focused on using nanoparticles such as silver and titanium dioxide for their antimicrobial properties, thereby improving food safety and prolonging shelf life. This field has seen significant advancements in synthesizing nanoparticles through various techniques, including electrospinning, mechanical milling, etching, and laser ablation. Additionally, nano barcodes on food products help ensure their safety and enable distribution tracking. The emerging field of food nanotechnology offers new opportunities to improve food quality and safety, provide valuable information to consumers and stakeholders throughout the supply chain, and enhance traceability and reduce food waste. However, concerns about nanoparticle toxicity and regulatory challenges must be addressed. This chapter highlights the future directions and emerging trends of food nanotechnology, emphasizing the need for continued research to ensure consumer safety and enhance the functional properties of food products.

items.title: FlashOffloading: Low-Latency KV Cache Offloading for Long-Context LLM Serving
items.abstract: In large language model (LLM) serving systems, the key-value (KV) cache grows linearly with sequence length and concurrency, so long-context inference easily hits the high-bandwidth memory (HBM) capacity wall and results in low concurrency. Offloading the KV cache to host dynamic random-access memory (DRAM) frees HBM space and raises concurrency, but the additional cache management and host-to-device (H2D) load overhead inflates inference latency, higher concurrency fails to translate into effective throughput. We present FlashOffloading, a host-DRAM-centric inference architecture that fully offloads the KV cache in both the prefill and decode phases. FlashOffloading builds rolling HBM cache for prefill, a hot cache for decode, a reverse sparse index with zero extra miss-lookup overhead, and a compute--load overlapped kernel, optimizing KV offloading latency across the entire pipeline and delivering throughput gains under a time-per-output-token (TPOT) service-level objective (SLO). In experiments deploying GLM-5.2 with multi-token prediction (MTP3) speculative decoding on an Ascend910C prefill--decode (PD)-disaggregated platform, FlashOffloading improves prefill throughput by up to 1.38\(\times\) and decode throughput by up to 1.91\(\times\) under a 30 ms TPOT constraint. FlashOffloading is integrated into an open-source serving framework: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm-ascend/tree/releases/v0.30.0.

items.title: Fermi-Level Modulation in Graphene Sensors Revealed by Voltage-Dependent Raman Spectroscopy and 3D Waterfall Response Mapping
items.abstract: Abstract The electronic properties of graphene sensors are governed by the position of the Fermi level, which determines the carrier concentration and consequently controls the electrical conductivity and sensing performance. Although Fermi-level modulation is widely recognized as the fundamental mechanism of graphene-based sensing, its direct experimental correlation with the dynamic sensing response has remained insufficiently explored. In this work, we demonstrate that Raman spectroscopy provides a direct, nondestructive method for quantifying the relative Fermi-level modulation through systematic shifts of the G and 2D Raman bands associated with changes in carrier concentration. The Raman analysis reveals reversible electrical tuning of the graphene electronic structure under source-drain voltage without introducing structural defects, allowing quantitative estimation of the Fermi-level relative displacement. To investigate the dynamic behavior of the same electronic states during sensor operation, low-frequency time–frequency waterfall spectroscopy was employed under chemical and optical stimulation. The results demonstrate that external stimuli induce transient perturbations of the graphene Fermi level, producing characteristic conductivity fluctuations that depend on the magnitude and kinetics of carrier-density modulation. The combination of static (Raman spectroscopy) and dynamic (waterfall fluctuation) analyses establishes a unified sensing mechanism linking Fermi-level modulation → carrier concentration → conductivity fluctuations → sensor response. These findings demonstrate that evaluation of the Fermi level is essential not only for understanding the intrinsic electronic structure of graphene but also for interpreting and optimizing its real-time chemical and optical sensing performance, providing a comprehensive framework for the design of next-generation graphene sensors.

items.title: Exploring the sustainable scaling of AI dilemma: a projective study of corporations’ AI environmental impacts
items.abstract: The rapid growth of artificial intelligence (AI), particularly Large Language Models (LLMs), raises environmental concerns extending beyond greenhouse gas emissions. Limited transparency from major providers hinders companies’ ability to evaluate their AI-related environmental impacts and achieve their net-zero targets. This paper proposes a methodology to estimate the environmental impact of a company’s AI portfolio, delivering actionable insights without requiring deep AI or Life-Cycle Assessment (LCA) expertise. Using a modeling approach that incorporates increased AI usage, hardware efficiency, and electricity mix changes aligned with IPCC (Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change) scenarios, we forecast AI impacts through 2030. Under a high adoption scenario, driven by complex generative AI models and frameworks, AI electricity consumption could rise by a factor of 24.4. Mitigating this impact by 2030 demands coordinated efforts across the AI value chain. Isolated measures like hardware or model efficiency alone are insufficient. We call for standardized environmental assessment frameworks, increased transparency, and a “Return on Environment” metric to align AI development with sustainability goals.

items.title: Enhancing Wheat Yield and Grain Zinc Content through Foliar Application of Zinc Sulfate under Clay Soil Conditions
items.abstract: Abstract Background : Since wheat is a primary staple food in Egypt, the bio-fortification of wheat grains with zinc serves as an effective strategy to increase dietary zinc intake and mitigate deficiency among the population. The purpose of this study is to investigate the effects of foliar application of zinc sulfate (ZnSO₄) at different growth stages on nutrient concentrations, particularly zinc as well as on growth characteristics, and performance of wheat yield. Materials and methods: Field experiments were conducted during the winter growth seasons 2019/2020 and 2020/2021 in the village of Kafr Al-Khadra, Al-Bagour District, Menoufia Governorate, Egypt. The location represents the typical Egyptian clay soil. The experiment included, two bread wheat (Triticum aestivum L.) Giza 171 and Gemeiza 11, arranged in a randomized complete block design (RCBD) with three replications. Each experimental plot measured 10.5 m² (3.5 m × 3.0 m). Foliar treatments consist of Zn sulfate (ZnSO 4 .7H 2 O) applied at a rate of 5 g/l during the stem elongation and milk-ripening stages. Large-scale, farmer-managed validation experiments were conducted during the winter growth seasons 2021/2022 and 2022/2023. Results: Foliar zinc application-particularly the double application significantly enhanced zinc Furthermore, the leaf foliar application of zinc sulfate (ZnSO₄) enhanced concentrations of potassium, calcium, magnesium, iron, and manganese in both grains and straw. Applying of ZnSO 4 twice with a concentration of 5 g L -1 during the stem elongation and milk-ripening stages increased grain yield by 13–15% compared to untreated control. In addition, the biological yield and harvest index have been significantly improved, while the concentration of zinc in grains has increased to a nutritionally meaningful significant level of approximately 47-54 ppm. Conclusion: The results confirmed a significant improvement in the concentration of zinc in grains and a markedly positive impact overall wheat yield.

items.title: Engineering relaxation timescales in Ag/SiO x /Pt volatile memristors via a thin Al 2 O 3 layer
items.abstract: Abstract Neuromorphic computing, exploiting time as a computational variable, needs the development of devices able to show rich dynamics over various timescales. Volatile electrochemical metallization (ECM) memristive devices are among the most promising candidates for this role thanks to their tunable relaxation dynamics, showing retention times typically in the ns to ms range. This paper investigates the complex relaxation timescales of Ag/SiO x /Pt volatile ECM devices emerging from the addition of a few nm thick Al 2 O 3 layer at the active interface. We show that, upon the insertion of the alumina layer, retention time increases up to several seconds and can be further extended with repetition of programming stimulation through a cumulative effect. The accumulation effect is reversible provided that the device is given enough time to recover. In summary, the overall device relaxation is composed of three different timescales, that can be controlled with programming parameters and alumina layer thickness and that we relate to different physical processes inside the device. Intrinsic retention is related to partial filament disruption in pristine (or recovered) devices; cumulative retention is caused by the incomplete dissolution of the filament inside Al 2 O 3 which causes, cycle after cycle, an increase in the retention time; recovery time is needed to recover intrinsic state in a previously stimulated device, and it is related to the retraction of the filament in the Al 2 O 3 layer. The latter two relaxation timescales, typically not reported in literature, can be exploited to implement neuronal and synaptic primitives thanks to their integrative nature.

items.title: Engineering Energy‐Storage Interfaces With Atomic and Molecular Layer Deposition: From Surface Chemistry to Process Design
items.abstract: ABSTRACT The performance and lifetime of energy‐storage devices are determined at the interfaces between electrodes, electrolytes, and separators, where ion and charge transfer, parasitic reactions, and mechanical degradation originate within nanometers of the surface. Atomic layer deposition (ALD) and molecular layer deposition (MLD) enable precise engineering of these interfaces through self‐limiting surface reactions that produce conformal coatings with controlled thickness and composition, even on porous electrodes. Although ALD surface chemistry is well established on ideal oxide surfaces, energy‐storage materials present chemically and structurally complex surfaces, on which reaction mechanisms, growth per cycle, and coating function can differ. This Review develops a chemistry–process–structure–function framework that connects surface chemistry, precursor reaction pathways, and nucleation behavior with film structure, ionic transport, charge‐transfer kinetics, redox stability, and mechanical response. We examine growth on oxide, sulfide, metal, polymer, and carbon substrates and relate the films to their functions at cathodes, anodes, solid electrolytes, and separators in Li‐based and beyond‐Li batteries. We further assess process scalability in terms of precursor utilization, throughput, and energy consumption, and discuss in situ monitoring, post‐deposition characterization, and full‐cell test conditions needed to validate coating performance. These relationships are summarized as six design rules presented as a decision flow.

items.title: Energy-Efficient Edge AI for Real-Time Anomaly Detection in IoT-Based Embedded Systems A Reproducible Comparison of Lightweight Detectors on Public Sensor Benchmarks
items.abstract: Energy-Efficient Edge AI for Real-Time Anomaly Detection in IoT-Based Embedded Systems A Reproducible Comparison of Lightweight Detectors on Public Sensor Benchmarks Rachit Debbad [India] Rishabh Misra[rishabheco@gmail.com] Abstract—Detecting abnormal sensor readings on the node itself saves bandwidth and latency, yet learned detectors are rarely compared on energy and memory cost alongside accuracy. This paper benchmarks eight lightweight unsupervised detectors — a rolling z-score, an EWMA control chart, PCA reconstruction, Isolation Forest, Local Outlier Factor (LOF), a one-class SVM, and a small autoencoder in FP32 and INT8 form on two public datasets: 52 labelled series of the Numenta Anomaly Benchmark (NAB; mixed server, traffic and sensor signals) and 34 runs of the Skoltech Anomaly Benchmark (SKAB; an eight-channel water-circulation sensor testbed). Models are fitted on the first 15% of each series without anomaly labels, and alarm thresholds come from training scores only. We report threshold-free and fixed-threshold metrics, bootstrap confidence intervals, paired tests, model memory, operation counts and a first-order analytic energy estimate (modelled, not measured on hardware). On NAB the learned detectors reach macro AUROC 0.56–0.58 and cannot be told apart statistically, but all clearly exceed the statistical baselines (0.49–0.50). On SKAB they reach 0.74–0.85 against 0.49–0.52. Cost differs by up to two orders of magnitude: under our model the INT8 autoencoder uses about 6× less energy than its FP32 form (4.6–20× across memory-cost assumptions) and 30–200× less than LOF, while weight quantization changes per-series AUROC by about 0.001. Fixed percentile thresholds transferred poorly on both datasets. The results favour compact reconstruction-based models for edge anomaly detection and identify hardware measurement and drift-aware thresholding as the necessary next steps. Keywords: edge AI; TinyML; anomaly detection; Internet of Things; embedded systems; autoencoder; quantization; energy efficiency; Numenta Anomaly Benchmark; Skoltech Anomaly Benchmark 1. Introduction IoT deployments place sensors where power is scarce and connectivity is costly. Streaming every raw reading to a cloud service for analysis consumes bandwidth and radio energy and adds latency, which is the usual motivation for moving analytics to the network edge [4]. For abnormal-reading detection (a failing bearing, a drifting thermistor, a blocked valve) the node itself must often decide, in real time, whether the latest window of samples is unusual. The anomaly-detection literature offers many methods [1]–[3], but evaluations typically rank them by accuracy alone. On a microcontroller the questions are different: how many bytes of model must live in flash or SRAM, how many arithmetic operations and memory fetches each decision costs, and whether the method survives reduced numeric precision. Work on resource-constrained learning, such as compact tree and nearest-neighbour models [13], [14], embedded inference runtimes [15] and the MLPerf Tiny benchmark [16], addresses the deployment side. It does not directly tell a designer how common detector families compare on public sensor-style data under one protocol, with quality and cost in the same table. This study provides such a hardware-free, reproducible comparison. Its contributions are: 1. A chronological, label-free training protocol and a common evaluation harness applied to two public datasets: 52 series of NAB [17] and 34 runs of the multivariate SKAB sensor testbed [26]. 2. A head-to-head comparison of eight lightweight detectors on threshold-free and fixed-threshold metrics, with bootstrap confidence intervals and paired significance tests. 3. A transparent cost model (memory footprint, multiply and add counts, estimated energy) that exposes the quality–cost trade-off, including an INT8 autoencoder and a sensitivity analysis of both the energy coefficients and the main design parameters. 4. An explicit account of limitations: modest absolute accuracy on NAB, poor transfer of percentile thresholds, small training sets on SKAB, and energy values that are modelled rather than measured. Section 2 reviews related work, Section 3 describes the methods and cost model, Section 4 the experimental setup, Section 5 the results, Section 6 discusses them together with limitations, and Section 7 concludes. 2. Related Work Anomaly-detection foundations. Chandola et al. [1] organise the field by data type and technique, and Blázquez-García et al. [2] do the same for time series, distinguishing point, subsequence and pattern anomalies. Pang et al. [3] review deep approaches. The detectors used here are classical representatives: control charts such as the EWMA chart [5]; isolation-based [6], density-based [7] and support-based [8] outlier detectors; and reconstruction-error methods, including autoencoders for sensor data [9]. Lightweight and on-device learning. Quantization-aware integer inference [11] and pruning with compression [12] reduce neural-network cost. Bonsai [13] and ProtoNN [14] are compact learners aimed at devices with kilobytes of memory. TensorFlow Lite Micro [15] provides an inference runtime for microcontrollers, and MLPerf Tiny [16] standardises tiny-model benchmarking, with an anomaly-detection task among its workloads. Kitsune [10] shows that ensembles of small autoencoders can run online for network intrusion detection. These works motivate our cost axes, but none compares the classical detector families above on public sensor-style data with quality and modelled cost side by side. Benchmarks and evaluation. The Numenta Anomaly Benchmark [17] provides labelled real and artificial streams with an application-oriented scoring scheme and was used to evaluate a streaming detector in [18]. SKAB [26] offers multivariate recordings from a water-circulation testbed with labelled fault episodes. Wu and Keogh [19] argue that several widely used time-series anomaly benchmarks suffer from triviality, mislabelling and other flaws that can exaggerate progress. We take that critique seriously: we avoid claims of state-of-the-art performance, report threshold-free metrics with confidence intervals, and caution against over-reading small differences. Energy modelling. Direct power measurement needs target hardware. A common first-order alternative counts arithmetic operations and memory accesses and weights them by per-operation energies, such as those summarised by Horowitz [20]. We adopt this approach and state its limits in Section 6.2. 3. Methodology 3.1 Problem formulation and pipeline A sensor emits a stream xt (a vector of C channels for SKAB). At each step the node normalises the sample with statistics from the training segment, forms a window of the last W normalised samples, and computes an anomaly score st. An alarm is raised when st exceeds a threshold τ (Eqs. 1–3). zt = (xt − μtr) / σtr (1) wt = (zt−W+1, …, zt) (2) alarmt = 1[ st > τ ] (3) Here μtr and σtr are the training-segment mean and standard deviation (per channel for SKAB), and τ is the 99th percentile of the scores st over the training segment. No anomaly labels are used for fitting or for choosing τ. Fig. 1 shows the pipeline. Fig. 1. Processing pipeline of the embedded anomaly detector. 3.2 Detectors Table 1 lists the eight detectors. The two statistical baselines process the normalised stream directly (for SKAB, per channel, with the maximum over channels as the score); the other methods use the window as a feature vector (W = 16 samples for NAB; W = 8 samples × 8 channels = 64 features for SKAB). Implementations use scikit-learn [21] defaults except where stated. Hyperparameters were fixed a priori and not tuned on the evaluation data. Table 1. Detector configurations (NAB / SKAB where they differ). Detector Configuration Anomaly score Rolling z-score trailing 64 samples, previous samples only |z − mean| / (std + 10⁻³); max over channels EWMA residual [5] smoothing factor 0.1 |z − EWMA| / (EW std + 10⁻³); max over channels PCA reconstruction 4 / 8 components mean squared reconstruction error Isolation Forest [6] 50 trees, 64 samples per tree negated scikit-learn score LOF [7] k = 20, novelty mode, ≤ 1000 stored windows negated LOF score One-class SVM [8] RBF kernel, gamma = "scale", ν = 0.05, ≤ 1000 windows negated decision function Autoencoder (FP32 / INT8) 16-8-4-8-16 / 64-16-8-16-64, ReLU hidden layers, linear output, Adam [22], learning rate 0.005, ≤ 300 epochs mean squared reconstruction error When a NAB series has more than 1000 training windows, 1000 are drawn at random (fixed seed) for fitting. SKAB training segments contain 104–192 windows (median 164) and are used in full. The z-score and EWMA baselines need no fitting. 3.3 INT8 autoencoder The INT8 variant applies post-training symmetric per-tensor quantization to every weight and bias matrix of the trained FP32 autoencoder, with scale s = max|W|/127 and values round(W/s) clipped to [−127, 127]. Accuracy is evaluated with the de-quantized weights. This simulates weight quantization only; activations stay in floating point, so end-to-end integer inference on a device may behave differently. The cost model treats the INT8 model as using 8-bit multiply-accumulates and 8-bit parameter storage. 3.4 Cost model For each detector we count stored bytes, multiplications, additions (comparisons count as additions) and 32-bit-word parameter reads per inference. items.title: Effect of PLA Molecular Weight on Mechanical and Morphological Properties of PVA/PLA Biomaterial Blown Films
items.abstract: This study investigates the influences of polylactic acid (PLA) molecular weight on mechanical behaviors and morphological property of polyvinyl alcohol (PVA)/PLA biomaterial blown films. Three commercial PLAs (L105, L130, and L175) with distinct molecular weights are individually blended with PVA at a fixed ratio of 50 wt%. Glycerol (20 phr) is employed as a plasticizer to enhance film processability. Films are fabricated via twin-screw extrusion followed by film blowing. Morphological observations confirm that interfacial adhesion and phase distribution are dependent on both PLA molecular weight and content. Mechanical analysis demonstrates that biomaterial PVA blown film with PLA L175 exhibit superior tensile strength and ductility due to improved interfacial entanglement. These findings highlight the critical role of interfacial interactions in tuning the structure–property relationship of PVA/PLA biomaterial systems, supporting their development as flexible, biodegradable films for advanced packaging applications.

items.title: Distributed Memory Management in Multi-tenant Clouds
items.abstract: Memory caches are critical components of modern web services: they absorb a large fraction of requests, reduce load on backend databases, and improve tail latency. In multi-tenant clouds, many independent cache tenants often share the same physical server and compete for a limited memory budget. Yet today’s common practice is to provision each tenant with a fixed memory allocation based on offline heuristics or peak estimates. Because tenant working sets and request rates change over time, static allocations are frequently suboptimal---some tenants suffer avoidable misses while others hold idle memory. Meanwhile, horizontal or vertical scaling is often slow, expensive, and operationally burdensome, requiring continual monitoring and manual retuning to keep up with workload dynamics. This dissertation develops a progression of systems that move from single-node to cluster-wide memory management for multi-tenant caches. Our first system, Tingo, takes an initial step toward distributed memory management by dynamically reallocating memory pages among co-located cache tenants, allowing memory-constrained tenants to adapt to workload changes and improve hit rates without manual scaling. Building on this direction, our second system, MemSweeper, more efficiently manages memory within a single server. MemSweeper introduces a score-based metric and allocation algorithm to identify tenants whose working sets have outgrown their current allocations and to safely reclaim memory from tenants whose working sets fit within their provisioned capacity with minimal impact to their hit rates. Across synthetic workloads and production traces, MemSweeper reduces the miss rate of memory-hungry tenants by an average of 74%. In our latest work, we enhance MemExchange to manage memory at cluster scope for environments that host both caching tenants and virtual machines (VMs). MemExchange removes the need for VM co-location to share capacity by unifying underutilized DRAM across servers into a logically shared pool that can be traded between tenants based on demand. It leverages RDMA for efficient remote memory access, allowing tenants to extend their effective cache capacity beyond a single machine with minimal overhead. To make reallocations practical at scale, we introduce the MemExchange Tracker Communication (MTC) protocol, a coordination mechanism that matches donors and receivers, schedules reallocations, and ensures tenants can seamlessly incorporate remote memory into their caching path. In a representative cluster/workload, MemExchange improves cache hit rates for memory-constrained tenants and increases overall cluster memory utilization by 15% relative to a static partitioning (no-trading) baseline.

items.title: DEQ-Det: Dual Evidence Queries for Few-Shot Analog IC Device Detection
items.abstract: Detecting analog integrated circuit (IC) devices in layout images supports circuit analysis and inspection. With only a few annotated examples, variation in device geometry and visual similarity to dummy or routing structures make reliable detection difficult. Foreground similarity alone can highlight plausible targets without distinguishing them from competing layout patterns. We propose Dual Evidence Queries for Detection (DEQ-Det), which constructs complementary foreground and background references from the same support images without additional annotations. Foreground references capture target morphology, while selected background references characterize surrounding layout patterns. Both sources guide query selection and region verification, combining target appearance with layout context. Across five held-out device categories and three random seeds, DEQ-Det achieves macro AP50 of 39.41 and 53.03 at 10 and 30 shots, exceeding the strongest listed baselines by 3.97 and 9.71 points, respectively. A matched 30-shot ablation further shows that RoI background evidence reduces pooled false positives at comparable recall, supporting its role in interference suppression.

items.title: Cu–Cu Grain Intermixing Quantification for Hybrid Bonding Applications
items.abstract: Cu–Cu hybrid bonding at reduced thermal budgets depends critically on reliable grain intermixing across the bonding interface. Yet interfacial evolution is still predominantly assessed qualitatively, precluding objective comparison across copper microstructures and process conditions. Here, we introduce Bond IQ, an automated image-based metrology framework that converts registered cross-sectional FIB-SEM datasets into physically interpretable descriptors using classical computer-vision methods. We apply the framework to five blanket chip-level pairings spanning three engineered copper microstructures: coarse-grain (CG), fine-grain locked (FG-L), and fine-grain thermally dynamic (FG-TD) Cu, thermocompression bonded at 210 °C for 2 h. Three coupled but distinct metrics are extracted: Bridged Interface Fraction (BIF), Interface Void Loading (IVL), and normalized Grain Penetration Depth (GPD). The symmetric CG/CG interface exhibited the weakest evolution, combining high IVL (5.4 nm) with low BIF (6.1%) and low GPD (0.20). By contrast, CG/FG-TD achieved the highest BIF (54.5%) at low IVL (0.6 nm), signifying broad but comparatively shallow bridging, whereas CG/FG-L reached the highest GPD (0.89) at moderate BIF (32.7%), indicating localized yet deeper directional grain advancement. Among symmetric fine-grained interfaces, FG-L/FG-L displayed the lowest IVL (0.5 nm), underscoring the role of fine-grain stability in void suppression. Collectively, these results demonstrate that interface bridging, void elimination, and penetration depth are governed by distinct but interrelated contributions of grain-size contrast and microstructural stability. By reducing subjective interfacial assessment to quantitative, mechanistically interpretable descriptors, Bond IQ offers a scalable route to screen copper microstructures and bonding conditions, and it can be extended to other metal–metal interfaces where microstructural evolution governs low-temperature bonding reliability.

items.title: Conveyor-mode electron shuttling through a T-junction in Si/SiGe
items.abstract: Abstract Conveyor-mode shuttling in gated Si/SiGe devices enables adiabatic transfer of single electrons, electron patterns and spin qubits confined in quantum dots across several microns with a scalable number of signal lines. To realize their full potential, linear shuttle lanes must connect into a two-dimensional grid with controllable routing. We introduce a T-junction device linking two independently driven shuttle lanes. Electron routing across the junction requires no extra control lines beyond the four channels per conveyor belt. We measure an inter-lane charge transfer fidelity of $$F={100.0000000}_{-9\times 1{0}^{-7}}^{+0}\,\%$$ F = 100.0000000 − 9 × 1 0 − 7 + 0 % at an instantaneous electron velocity of 270 mm s −1 . The filling of 54 quantum dots is controlled by simple atomic pulses, allowing us to swap electron patterns, laying the groundwork for a native spin-qubit SWAP gate. This T-junction establishes a path towards scalable, two-dimensional quantum computing architectures with flexible spin qubit routing for quantum error correction.

items.title: Consumer Perception and Acceptance of Nanotechnology in Food
items.abstract: Nanotechnology (NT) has significant potential to transform the food industry by enhancing safety, quality, and sustainability. However, the successful development and commercialisation of nanoformulated food products are strongly influenced by consumer perception and acceptance. Limited public awareness of NT raises concerns regarding health risks, environmental impact, safety, and ethical considerations. This chapter critically evaluates consumer perception and acceptance of NT applications in food processing and packaging. It synthesises existing research, including survey-based studies, to assess current knowledge across key domains such as nano-ingredients and additives, nanostructured foods, nanosensors, and advanced packaging systems (including active packaging, antimicrobial nanoparticles, and nanomaterials). The analysis further examines determinants of consumer acceptance, including awareness levels, perceived risks and benefits, demographic and cultural factors, economic considerations, trust in regulatory frameworks, and transparency in labelling. The chapter explores effective communication strategies to improve public understanding and acceptance, including risk communication, educational initiatives, transparent labelling practices, and stakeholder engagement. The findings provide valuable insights for researchers, industry stakeholders, and policymakers to address consumer concerns and facilitate the responsible adoption of NT in the food sector.

items.title: Considerations for Bond Strength Metrology and Standards
items.abstract: Chevron based bond strength structures provide significant advantages over the double cantilever beam method commonly in use. We introduce new bond strength test structure designs with the goal of simplifying the implementation of the chevron test and improving the availability of bond strength metrology. We describe designs based on chip-to-chip bonding which could be expanded to chip to wafer. There are both asymmetric bond structures based on separate designs for the top and bottom chips and symmetric designs in which the same chip design serves as both top and bottom. We describe a fabrication process which is compatible with both blanket dielectric and metal bonding surfaces as well as patterned surfaces including hybrid bonding type materials. We also describe a testing apparatus and the potential to adapt commercial die shear testers for this measurement. Finally, we describe a plan to realize research grade test materials based on these test structures.

items.title: Comparative Analysis and Genetic Algorithm Optimization of Multi-Transistor FinFET SRAM Topologies for SNM, Leakage, and Delay Improvement at 18nm
items.abstract: With continuous technology scaling, Static Random Access Memory (SRAM) faces significant challenges including increased leakage power, reduced stability, and higher delay. FinFET technology has emerged as a promising alternative to conventional CMOS technology due to its superior electrostatic control and reduced short-channel effects. This paper presents a multi-objective Genetic Algorithm (GA) optimization framework for 6T, 7T, 8T, 9T, and 10T SRAM architectures using 18nm FinFET technology. The proposed optimization methodology focuses on minimizing leakage power, dynamic power, read delay, and write delay while maximizing Static Noise Margin (SNM). Cadence Virtuoso and the Spectre simulator were used for transient, DC, and power analysis. Genetic Algorithm optimization was implemented using transistor sizing and fin-count optimization techniques. The optimized SRAM architectures demonstrated significant reductions in leakage and dynamic power at a reduced supply voltage (1 V versus 1.5 V), with lower noise margins and a mixed effect on propagation delay. Simulation results show that optimized 10T SRAM achieved the lowest leakage power while 9T SRAM exhibited the highest read stability.

items.title: Collapsing Silicon Hegemony: Backend RISC-V Erosion, SoftBank LTV Margin Contagion, and Deterministic QFS-zkVM Interlocks for Post-Arm AI Infrastructure
items.abstract: Modern computational infrastructure has historically rested on the surface tension of a single proprietary Instruction Set Architecture (ISA): the Arm licensing ecosystem. However, as of 2026, two irreversible structural fractures have invalidated this hegemony: (1) Qualcomm's decisive final judgment victory over Arm in the U.S. District Court for the District of Delaware (September 30, 2025), which neutralized intellectual property intimidation over Architectural License Agreements (ALAs); and (2) Arm's predatory pivot into selling finished 136-core 3nm silicon ("Arm AGI CPU"), creating an irreconcilable conflict of interest with hyperscale licensees (AWS Graviton, Google Axion, Microsoft Cobalt). Concurrently, compiler-level hardware abstraction via OpenAI Triton, JAX/XLA, and PolyBlocks, combined with system-level Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures such as Microsoft's 1-trillion-parameter MAI-Thinking-1, has rendered proprietary frontend ISAs economically obsolete. Hyperscalers and sovereign-scale initiatives—most notably the $500 billion, 10-gigawatt Stargate Project—now face an existential mandate to eliminate multi-billion-dollar Arm royalty deadweight losses by transitioning backend compute to open RISC-V Vector Extension (RVV) chiplets and constant-stride EARTH memory architectures. This monograph formalizes the four-phase financial and physical contagion triggered by the collapse of Arm's growth terminal value: (Phase I) Valuation contraction of Arm shares; (Phase II) Breach of the 25% Loan-to-Value (LTV) threshold across SoftBank Group's (SBG) $18.5 billion Arm-backed margin loans alongside its $40 billion unsecured bridge debt (CDS spread at 355 bps); (Phase III) Forced liquidation of AI equity portfolios; and (Phase IV) Stranded-asset collapse across crypto-mining facilities that pivoted $65 billion into non-interruptible AI High-Performance Computing (HPC) data centers, culminating in forced Bitcoin treasury liquidations. To insulate sovereign AI and energy grids from this cascading failure, we introduce a deterministic hardware-cryptographic governance architecture integrating Real-Time Optimization (RTO P2.0), the Quantum Financial System Zero-Knowledge Virtual Machine (QFS-zkVM) over the 64-bit Goldilocks prime field $\mathbb{F}_p$ ($p = 2^{64}-2^{32}+1$), Q-SAFA cryptographic attestation, PHOENIX_BRIDGE / PHOENIX_ROUTER autonomous load-shedding, and Human-in-Command (HIC) statutory interlocks enforcing SEC Rule 15c3-5 and Delaware Caremark fiduciary oversight. items.title: Co-optimization of spin coherence and valley splitting in Si/SiGe heterostructures
items.abstract: Single electron spins can be used to encode and process information in semiconductor quantum devices. Progress has been hindered by materials challenges, such as the small energy splitting between low-lying valley states and hyperfine coupling to nuclear spins. Here we use density functional theory to optimize the valley splitting and spin dephasing time in realistic Si/SiGe heterostructures. Reductions in the Si quantum well width generally increase the valley splitting. However, in narrow quantum wells, a larger fraction of the electronic wavefunction resides in the SiGe buffer layers, which increases the hyperfine coupling with spinful $^{73}$Ge. Our work shows that Si/SiGe heterostructures with 3~--~4~nm wide quantum wells and $^{73}$Ge and $^{29}$Si concentrations of 50 ppm should support average valley splittings $E_{v}$~$>$~500~$μ$eV and spin dephasing times $T_2^*$ exceeding 15~$μ$s assuming an effective quantum dot area of 700 nm$^2$. In addition, sharper Si/SiGe interfaces in general result in larger valley splittings and longer spin dephasing times.

items.title: Charge Retention in Lunar Regolith: Microscopic Processes and Constraints on Subsurface Charging
items.abstract: Energetic-particle irradiation can produce persistent charge separation within lunar regolith, but the internal fields predicted by subsurface-charging models depend on how particle interactions are translated into retained charge. This critical review examines the evidence and assumptions connecting microscopic charge formation to macroscopic charging. We distinguish energy deposition, net charge transfer across a specified boundary, and the spatial distribution of signed excess charge. We organize these distinctions using an average retained-charge response defined for specified material, irradiation, electrical-state, and evaluation conditions. Its use as a volumetric source requires consistent charge accounting, compatible incident-flux definitions, and an adequate separation between response formation and subsequent transport. Applying these criteria to existing models, emission studies, and silicate irradiation experiments yields three assessments. First, emission measurements constrain electron loss across the measured boundary but do not locate internally redistributed charge. Second, evidence of internal reabsorption does not by itself establish that the charge separation sustaining subsurface fields is reduced; an illustrative calculation shows that the same net charge supply can produce different peak fields depending on transfer depths. Third, laboratory electrical damage in silicate crystals does not determine breakdown rates in cryogenic, porous regolith, which additionally require constraints on local fields, failure properties, and discharge recurrence. Joint constraints on boundary charge transfer, spatial charge separation, and post-irradiation relaxation are central to evaluating lunar subsurface-charging predictions.

items.title: Calibrated Facial Photography Protocol for Digital Prosthetic Planning.
items.abstract: Facial esthetic analysis constitutes a fundamental element in contemporary dental diagnosis and treatment planning. The spatial orientation of the maxilla serves as the cornerstone of such assessments. Conventional analog techniques employing anatomic facebows are susceptible to positioning errors resulting from craniofacial asymmetries. In contrast, digital workflows integrating facial photographs and intraoral scans accurately, offer enhanced precision. However, reliability may be compromised by head posture, camera angulation, image manipulation, etc. This article introduces a Calibrated Facial Photography (CFP) protocol aimed at standardizing facial image acquisition in Natural Head Position (NHP). The protocol encompasses four sequential stages: NHP establishment, photograph capture using external calibration references, digital image editing and alignment, and 2D-3D integration within computer-aided design environments. By objectively quantifying the angular discrepancy between the interpupillary line and the true horizontal plane in NHP, the CFP protocol differentiates between negligible (0-2°) and significant (≥2°) deviations. This method reduces subjective operator bias, enhances the reproducibility of digital facial records, and improves the accuracy of prosthetically guided rehabilitation. CFP represents a cost-effective, accessible and simple approach to optimize precision in digital dental workflows.

items.title: An on-glass a-IGZO TFT operational amplifier for local voltage regulation in display driving systems
items.abstract: This work presents an on-glass amorphous indium-gallium-zinc oxide thin-film transistor (a-IGZO TFT) operational amplifier to achieve an integrated local voltage-regulation for reference-voltage stabilization in display driving systems. The fabricated op-amp adopts compact n-type-only two-stage architecture to reduce circuit complexity and internal high-impedance nodes for closed-loop operation. Under ± 15 V supply voltages, the measured op-amp exhibits a voltage gain of 35.5 dB, a cut-off frequency of 5.8 kHz, and a unit-gain frequency of 39 kHz. To examine closed-loop controllability, the op-amp was combined with external pass/load components in a prototype regulation setup. The measured output voltages were 1.82 V, 3.79 V, and 5.55 V for reference voltages of 2 V, 4 V, and 6 V, respectively. Circuit-level simulations were further used to analyze line-ripple suppression and load-transient recovery. The results indicate that a-IGZO TFT op-amps can be useful analog building blocks for low-current local voltage regulation in system-on-glass display platforms.

items.title: Aminophosphonium Dihydrogen Phosphate: A Structurally Modified KDP Analogue With Room‐Temperature Ferro‐ and Piezoelectric Properties
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Potassium dihydrogen phosphate is well‐known to exhibit ferroelectricity, while ammonium dihydrogen phosphate is an antiferroelectric material, with both of them exhibiting a phase transition to paraelectric phase below room temperature. In this work, we report the synthesis and room‐temperature ferroelectric behavior of an aminophosphonium dihydrogen phosphate of formula, [{P(NHPh) 4 (H 2 PO 4 )·(CH 3 OH) 0.5 ] ( TAPDP·(CH 3 OH) 0.5 ) that exhibits a three‐dimensional pillared‐layered hydrogen bonding network. (TAPDP·(CH 3 OH) 0.5 crystallizes in the polar monoclinic P 2 1 space group, and its non‐centrosymmetric structure was confirmed by second‐harmonic generation (SHG) measurements. The ferroelectric behavior was further verified through polarization–electric field ( P–E ) loop measurements, with a saturation polarization of 21.40 µC cm −2 . Structural analysis combined with preliminary density functional theory calculations indicates a ferrielectric‐type ordering in which the adjacent layers exhibit different polarization directions but with unequal dipole moments. Furthermore, the electromechanical energy‐harvesting properties of TAPDP·(CH 3 OH) 0 . 5 were explored in its composites with the polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) polymer. The 10 wt% TAPDP·(CH 3 OH) 0 . 5 – PDMS device exhibited a maximum peak‐to‐peak open‐circuit voltage (𝑉 oc ) of 10.69 ± 0.04 V and the output work efficiency parameter (OWE) of 9.63%. Owing to the superior signal sensitivity of this device, a contact‐type sensor was developed to measure a motor's revolutions per minute (RPM) at both low and high speeds.

items.title: A superhard and ultra-wide bandgap tetragonal C3N2 featuring a deep-ultraviolet isotropic point
items.abstract: The pursuit of materials that simultaneously exhibit superhard mechanical behavior and ultra‑wide bandgap semiconductor characteristics remains a critical challenge for next‑generation precision deep-ultraviolet (DUV) optics and extreme-condition applications. Here, we report P4 2 /nmc -C 3 N 2 , a novel tetragonal carbon nitride phase predicted and validated by first‑principles calculations. This structure features a three‑dimensional covalent network with four‑coordinated carbon and three‑coordinated nitrogen atoms. Formation enthalpy calculations show that P4 2 /nmc -C 3 N 2 becomes thermodynamically stable against decomposition into graphite and N 2 above 28 GPa, indicating its feasibility for high‑pressure high‑temperature synthesis. The material exhibits an indirect ultra-wide bandgap of 4.27 eV and a macroscopic Vicker’s hardness of 47.7 GPa, placing it in the superhard regime. Notably, P4 2 /nmc -C 3 N 2 possesses highly anisotropic mechanical and optical properties. Its hole effective mass along the [001] direction is only 0.545 m 0 , significantly smaller than those of GaN and ZnO and comparable to hexagonal boron nitride, suggesting a potential advantage for p‑type doping. Furthermore, the calculated optical response reveals an isotropic point at ~5.2 eV (238 nm) with zero birefringence near the transparency threshold, offering a unique mechanism for narrow-band isotropic filtering and distortion-free deep-ultraviolet optics. These characteristics make P4 2 /nmc -C 3 N 2 a promising multifunctional material bridging superhardness and tailored anisotropic optical functionality.

items.title: A High‐Speed Dielectric Approach to Track Domain Structure Evolution in Operating Ferroelectric Devices
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Ferroelectric switching is a fundamental process underpinning the functionality of modern electronic devices, yet the dynamic evolution of ferroelectric domain structures, especially in thin films, remains poorly understood. While established techniques such as piezoresponse force microscopy and transmission electron microscopy successfully image ferroelectric domains, they fail to capture global transient domain dynamics due to resolution limits and slow acquisition. In addition, performing in operando measurements on functional devices is highly impractical with these methods. This gap has hindered progress in understanding and controlling ferroelectric switching in thin films, which is critical for applications from nonvolatile memories to sensors. Here, we introduce a novel approach using amplitude‐modulated dielectric signals in the frequency domain to drastically reduce acquisition times to microseconds, instead of seconds. This method allows real‐time, nondestructive, and in operando tracking of domain wall density and mobility in ferroelectric devices, overcoming the limitations of existing techniques. By applying this approach to (Ba,Ca)TiO 3 thin films, we directly probe transient states in response to electric pulses, revealing previously inaccessible dynamics. This breakthrough opens new avenues for studying dynamic domain switching in thin films and promises to advance the design of ferroelectric materials for next‐generation electronic devices.

items.title: A CE-C4D Platform Integrating 3D-Printer Ecosystems, Luer-Standard Pneumatics, and Open-Source Hardware
items.abstract: Capillary electrophoresis with Capacitively Coupled Contactless Conductivity Detection (CE-C4D) offers high analytical efficiency and low sample consumption. However, commercial instrumentation remains cost-prohibitive for resource-limited or citizen science settings. Here, we report the design, fabrication, and experimental validation of a low-cost, modular CE-C4D platform based on open hardware architectures (dual C4D, Arduino, RAMPS, and syringe pump modules), FDM 3D-printed parts, 3D printer hardware, Luer-standard medical supplies for pneumatic integrity, and a commercial DC–DC converter. Pressure-driven flow tests demonstrated excellent pneumatic and hydrodynamic stability, yielding variation coefficients below 0.5% for displaced sample plugs. Low-pressure Dual-Opposite Injections of nanoliter-scale sample plugs were implemented using custom hollow-electrode manifolds and a motorized medical three-way valve. Operating under suppressed electroosmotic flow in 2.3 M acetic acid, simultaneous separation of inorganic ions (K+, Ca2+, Mg2+, NO3−, Cl−, SO42−) was achieved in synthetic and commercial hydroponic nutrient samples in less than 5 min for single-detector readings and 12 min for dual-point detection. Dual-point detection enables in-line auto-verification of assay validity, continuously confirming electromigration velocity, peak identity, and hydrodynamic consistency. The hardware achieves reliable run-to-run repeatability and robust fluidic control, providing an accessible, replicable instrument foundation for decentralized chemical profiling and quantitative analytical methods.

items.title: Enabling AWS Cloud FPGA Development Using High-Level Vitis HLS
items.abstract: We present a toolchain for development of ML models on AWS EC2 F2 cloud FPGA infrastructure from high-level language, implementing a complete Vitis HLS to HDK bridge to AFI workflow that has been absent from the academic literature despite eight years of AWS FPGA availability. We introduce a four-level methodology (FP32 PyTorch, bit-accurate quantized Python, HLS C-simulation, physical FPGA) to aid in localizing errors, including FPGA-specific circuit errors. Together these tools allow coding agents to effectively implement FPGA designs from user directions, testing and debugging as needed. We document the deployment workflow, timing closure strategies, and practical HLS engineering decisions that proved crucial. We validate using TinyBERT fine-tuned for address Named Entity Recognition, implementing the embedding layer and the first of four encoder layers on the FPGA hardware. Our implementation streams weights from host DRAM, yielding poor performance compared to CPU/GPU implementations; we discuss forward paths.

items.title: PIMROP: A Feasibility Study of Return-Oriented Programming on Commercial Processing-in-Memory Architectures
items.abstract: Processing-in-Memory places small programmable cores on the memory device, where they execute beside the DRAM banks and beyond the control-flow defenses that protect host programs. The security of this in-memory code is an attack surface that remains largely unstudied. We present PIMROP, to our knowledge the first demonstrated code-reuse attack on a commercial Processing in-Memory ISA. We show that return-oriented programming is feasible on a real, commercially shipped PIM instruction set, the UPMEM DPU, whose DRAM Processing Units run C compiled by a dedicated LLVM toolchain. We build Galileo-for-DPU, a gadget scanner adapted to the DPU's fixed-width, 8-byte-aligned RISC encoding, and run it entirely on the UPMEM functional simulator in a reproducible Docker and VM environment. We find the runtime library that every kernel links already yields 517 non-trivial gadgets covering all five canonical ROP primitive classes, and all 13 PrIM benchmarks we scanned carry gadgets as well. We then demonstrate two verified end-to-end attacks, each reproducible on 10 of 10 runs. In the first, a stack buffer overflow in a DPU kernel overwrites the saved return address and diverts control into a routine that copies a secret into host-readable memory. In the second, we leak the same secret using a chain of reused gadgets alone, without diverting control into any such routine. We further show that two standard defenses--stack canaries and _FORTIFY_SOURCE-style bounds-check fortification--fail on the DPU in ways specific to the platform (misplaced canary, silently inactive wrapper), and we verify a bounds-checked DMA that stops the attack on 10 of 10 runs with no effect on benign requests. To enable further research on PIM security, we open-source Galileo-for-DPU and our testing harness at https://github.com/wtegge2/ROP-in-PIM.

items.title: 可编程忆阻芯片的误差阻断与宽冗余设计:SM离散判据框架
items.abstract: 摘要 多电平与模拟忆阻芯片的规模化受制于随机电报噪声、漂移与工艺变异:噪声减小档间余量,漂移侵蚀已写状态,变异打散档位分布。主流方案是事后纠错与补偿(写验证、ECC、漂移软件补偿),成本随档位数上升。本文给出SM离散判据框架:档位归约判据|G−nG0|≤Δ/2、设计裕度Δ≥6σ(误判率≤0.27%)、边界歧义显式化;据此提出三级误差监测抑制机制(L1档位判读监控、L2裕度阻断、L3在线自适应补偿)与宽冗余自适应器件设计原则——不必让材料精密,用结构判据设计容差。全部判据可复算;预言B(Δ≥6σ→误判率≤0.27%)附单器件、参数分析仪、半天可完成的验证协议(§5.3)。 Abstract Scaling multi-level and analogue memristive chips is limited by random telegraph noise, drift and process variation: noise narrows the inter-level margin, drift erodes the written state, and variation smears the level distribution. The prevailing approach is after-the-fact correction and compensation through write verification, error-correcting codes and software drift compensation, whose cost rises with the number of levels. This paper gives an SM discrete-criterion framework: the level-reduction criterion bounding the conductance deviation, the design margin of six sigma with a misjudgement rate at most 0.27 per cent, and an explicit treatment of boundary ambiguity. On this basis a three-level error monitoring and suppression mechanism is proposed, comprising L1 level-read monitoring, L2 margin blocking and L3 on-line adaptive compensation, together with design principles for wide-redundancy adaptive devices: the material need not be precise if the tolerance is designed through structural criteria. All criteria are recomputable, and Prediction B, that six sigma implies a misjudgement rate at most 0.27 per cent, is accompanied by a verification protocol that a single device, a parameter analyser and half a day are sufficient to complete. 本记录当前为中文版(Chinese version);英文版将作为新版本追加(English version to follow as a new version)。

items.title: The Ideal Switch®: Glass-based Device With Demonstrated Reliability
items.abstract: Menlo Microsystems Inc. (Menlo Micro) has introduced a MEMS switch that utilizes both a glass substrate and a glass cap with through glass via (TGV) technology to provide an all-glass packaging solution. The MEMS switch technology combined with an all- glass packaging solution, has resulted in the Ideal Switch®. It is the world’s smallest, most reliable, and efficient micro-mechanical switch that can be used for numerous RF and power applications. The Ideal Switch® gains superior performance as well as mechanical, electrical and thermal reliability from several aspects of the MEMS and glass packaging design including robust electrical contacts, low electrical loss of glass, and hermetic TGVs which provide a well-controlled environment. This controlled environment is crucial for attaining reliable performance over billions of cycles. In addition to long lifetimes, parasitics are reduced by >75% vs. Si based RF devices enabling the devices to have a wide operational bandwidth from DC to > 50 GHz and high signal integrity. To enable the volume manufacture of this device, Menlo Micro has driven advancements in the glass supply chain over the past several years, leveraging mostly standard semiconductor manufacturing processes, on glass substrates (with and without TGV). In addition to hermetic TGV, the device contains multi-layer plated and deposited structures, hermetic wafer level glass to glass bonding, post-bond die singulation and device packaging in multiple formats. These devices pass standard JEDEC reliability testing and have operational lifetime in excess of 3 billion cycles. In this presentation we will discuss a number of advanced packaging processes employed by Menlo Micro in the manufacturing process in a volume manufacturing environment as well as key performance metrics of the Ideal Switch®. We will also discuss some early failure modes seen from this glass-based device in both device and packaged form, and how Menlo Micro has established solutions and demonstrated reliable performance relative to JEDEC standards.

items.title: Super‐Paraelectric Regulation of Energy Storage Performance in Sm 2 O 3 ‐Doped (Ba,Sr)TiO 3 Films via Nanostructure Engineering
items.abstract: ABSTRACT This work presents a strategy for enhancing the energy storage performance in BaTiO 3 ‐based nanocomposite films through a super‐paraelectric regulation approach enabled by Sm 2 O 3 doping. The proposed lead‐free (1‐ x )(Ba 0.8 Sr 0.2 )TiO 3 ‐ x Sm 2 O 3 (0.0 ≤ x ≤ 0.5) films contain only five elements, making them environmentally friendly and simple in composition. The incorporation of Sm 2 O 3 as an immiscible second phase within the (Ba 0.8 Sr 0.2 )TiO 3 matrix induces significant chemical and structural heterogeneity, inducing a transition from a conventional ferroelectric state to a super‐paraelectric state. In combination with an enhanced breakdown strength, this design results in an ultrahigh energy storage efficiency ( η ) exceeding 80%, along with a remarkable recoverable energy storage density ( U e ) of 50.6 and 59.2 J/cm 3 at Sm 2 O 3 contents of x = 0.4 and 0.5. Furthermore, the films with x = 0.4 and 0.5 exhibit superior frequency (20 Hz to 5 kHz) and thermal stability (25°C–160°C), highlighting exceptional operational reliability and robustness under varying conditions. This study demonstrates that the proposed super‐paraelectric regulation strategy provides a practical pathway for designing compositionally optimized and eco‐friendly energy storage materials.

items.title: Separating Motion Artifacts from Biomarker Signals in Flexible MoS2 FET Cortisol Sensors: A Coupled Multiphysics Model and Finite-Element Analysis of Strain-Binding Cross-Talk and Mitigation Strategies
items.abstract: Abstract Flexible molybdenum disulfide (MoS2) field-effect transistor (FET) biosensors can monitor cortisol in sweat, but their atomically thin channel is strongly piezoresistive, so body movement produces current changes that resemble hormone signals. We present a six-stage multiphysics model that links wrist and elbow flexion and walking to a strain-equivalent false cortisol concentration. Channel strain is computed by plane-strain finite-element analysis in the open-source solver Elmer, verified against laminate beam theory, and drives compact models of piezoresistance, Schottky-barrier lowering, strain-binding cross-talk, aptamer kinetics and Debye screening. For a 25 µm polyimide patch the model predicts wrist flexion produces a current artifact of 44% of the full-scale cortisol response and walking 5 to 11 ng/mL of false cortisol, with about 70% of the artifact arising at the Schottky contacts. Low-pass filtering leaves the non-zero mean of unipolar flexion (22% of full scale). Twin-sensor subtraction is limited by gauge mismatch and by a cross-talk floor proportional to aptamer occupancy, 1.0 to 2.8% of full scale across the physiological range at the wrist. With a 2.5 µm substrate and matched twin channels the residual falls to 0.9 to 1.3 ng/mL, not consistently below a 1 ng/mL target at the wrist for the assumed affinity. A rigid island under the channel retains 18 to 109% of the baseline strain under end-moment loading and about 300% when the skin imposes the curvature, so it fails to isolate the channel in bending. The predicted magnitudes scale with the assumed threshold shift; design guidelines by body location are given.

items.title: NN-Based FeFET Compact Modeling for SPICE Simulation
items.abstract: Prototyping and early-stage circuit evaluation for emerging transistor technologies require fast and accurate compact models for SPICE simulations. Standard physics-based compact models, such as BSIM, offer high fidelity but demand extensive domain expertise and time-consuming equation formulation for every new physical effect, significantly slowing technology development. Neural network (NN)-based models offer a scalable alternative approach, but they rely heavily on smooth numerical solver data with explicit high-order derivative information. However, measurement data suffers from complex noise patterns, making derivative extraction challenging and complicating NN-based transistor modeling. This work presents a derivative-free NN training framework employing spectral normalization to naturally smooth derivative behavior and filter measurement noise. Using drain current measurements from a fabricated 28 nm ferroelectric device, we design an NN-based compact model that captures the full spectrum of polarization amplitudes and supports dynamic polarization switching in transient simulations. To demonstrate its capability, we deploy the model in a commercial SPICE software to simulate write and read operations for large-scale memory arrays with up to 512x512 size, including parasitic effects. Our approach bridges raw measurements with NN-based SPICE-compatible transistor modeling, significantly reducing model development time and enabling rapid circuit-level prototyping for emerging devices.

items.title: Metrology challenges and trends for through-glass vias in advanced semiconductor packaging
items.abstract: Abstract Through-glass vias (TGVs) are emerging as a key technology for three-dimensional heterogeneous integration and advanced semiconductor packaging because of their low electrical loss, tailorable thermal expansion, and compatibility with large-format panel-level processing. However, the optical transparency, refractive properties, and brittleness of glass create significant inspection challenges, making reliable high-throughput metrology a major barrier to TGV manufacturing. This review presents a requirements-driven framework for TGV metrology that links fabrication processes and defect mechanisms to quantitative measurement needs. Key defects associated with laser ablation, laser-induced deep etching, and metallization including microcracks, nanovoids, sidewall roughness, via taper, copper protrusion, and thermomechanical cracking are examined. Representative metrology requirements include detection of sub-1-µm microcracks and sub-2-µm voids, characterization of sidewall roughness below 50 nm, taper-angle uncertainty below 0.1°, and panel-scale inspection at thousands of vias per second. Established and emerging techniques, including shadowgraphy, optical coherence tomography (OCT), spectral reflectometry, digital holographic microscopy (DHM), and two-photon fluorescence, are compared in terms of measurement capability, uncertainty, calibration, traceability, and throughput. No single technique currently meets the combined requirements for resolution, field of view, defect sensitivity, and high-volume throughput. Multimodal inspection, AI-assisted defect classification, physics-informed reconstruction, virtual metrology, and TGV-specific reference artefacts and standards are therefore identified as key directions toward robust, traceable, and scalable TGV metrology.

items.title: Interchannel Coupling in Two-Channel THz Detectors]{Interchannel Coupling in Two-Channel AlGaN/GaN Plasmonic Terahertz Detectors
items.abstract: Abstract A second two-dimensional electron gas (2DEG) forms in AlGaN/GaN high-electron-mobility transistors (HEMTs) capped with AlN. The strong response of measured double-channel terahertz (THz) detectors has been attributed to the coupling between the channels, but a measured responsivity also contains the antenna coupling and the bias, so whether the coupling itself helps is not known. We isolate the coupling by modelling plasma-wave rectification in this detector and in uncapped and GaN-capped single-channel references. A semi-analytical theory, to our knowledge the first for rectification in asymmetric coupled channels, joins analytic coupled eigenmodes of the gated region to transmission-line access regions and splits the photovoltage exactly into modal terms. A full-device perturbation model adds Schr\"odinger--Poisson and two-dimensional electrostatics, a floating drain and hot electrons. A nonlinear time-domain solver verifies its implementation within 3.0\% over 375 cases, the model reproduces the Dyakonov--Shur limit within 0.4\%, and a Boltzmann (Mermin) estimate keeps kinetic corrections below 0.3\% at zero bias. We find that in these AlN-capped devices the coupling does not help. For matched, conjugate or direct antenna coupling and a floating drain, the single-channel devices respond best (0.22--0.28\,V/W at 1\,THz, against 0.10\,V/W). A design map over upper-channel mobility and barrier thickness shows that a better upper channel makes the detector worse: it shunts the access regions and lowers the device impedance, while the rectification itself changes little. Toward threshold the small-signal noise-equivalent power falls to about 20--23\,pW/$\sqrt{\rm Hz}$ in the hydrodynamic model. Both models apply to other stacks of capacitively coupled channels.

items.title: Fluorine surface engineering for Vt control and memory window boost in HZO FeFET toward high-performance, energy-efficient in-memory computing
items.abstract: Threshold-voltage (V t ) control without sacrificing the memory window remains a key challenge for energy-efficient ferroelectric field-effect transistor (FeFET)-based in-memory computing. Here, we introduce a novel fluorine surface treatment (FST)-based V t tuning strategy that selectively engineers the interfacial layer of Hf 0.5 Zr 0.5 O 2 based Si FeFETs.
