Fluorine-induced electrostatic modulation and interfacial defect passivation jointly contribute to a positive shift of the entire transfer hysteresis and memory-window enhancement without noticeably altering the ferroelectric switching characteristics of the HZO layer. The optimized FST achieves an approximately 0.5 V positive V t shift, an approximately 0.5 V memory window enhancement, and a 40× reduction in leakage current at 0 V, enabling normally-off operation of the low-V t state. The resulting devices exhibit robust reliability, consistent device-to-device characteristics, and favorable analog synaptic behavior. Furthermore, simulation using the experimentally measured device characteristics improves CIFAR-10 classification accuracy from approximately 78% to 83%. These results establish interfacial-layer-selective fluorine engineering as a compelling route toward low-leakage, reliable, and energy-efficient FeFET-based analog in-memory computing.

items.title: Ferroelectricity and Peierls transition in MOI$_2$ (M=Ta, Nb): a first-principle analysis
items.abstract: The van der Waals ferroelectric NbOI$_2$ hosts a polar distortion that is commonly attributed to the Peierls dimerization of its Nb chains. Here we show, using first-principles calculations and a Landau-type energy, that the polar instability is in fact a distinct order parameter that does not stem from the Peierls mode condensation and that three main distinct modes are important in the whole MOI$_2$ family. They are a polar mode $P$, an antipolar mode $η$, and a Peierls mode $δ$, whose stabilities and couplings strongly depend on the nature of the $M$ metal element, as evidenced by the fact that the isostructural, TaOI$_2$ system is not polar while possessing Peirls distortions.

items.title: Ferroelectric Topological Structures: From Discovery to Functional Manipulation
items.abstract: Abstract The introduction of topology has opened up a whole new way of looking at complex ordered states in condensed matter. Ferroelectrics, with their spontaneous polarization as the order parameter, can, under specific boundary conditions, form nontrivial polar textures, especially the polar topological structures (the electric counterparts of the topological spin structures), including flux-closures, vortices, skyrmions, merons, and even hopfions. These polar topological textures come with intriguing functionalities like negative capacitance and chiral optical responses, making them promising building blocks for next generation high density storage and neuromorphic computing. In this review, we trace the evolution of polar topological textures in ferroelectrics from the early experimental breakthroughs to the emergence of diverse material platforms. We examine the design strategies for hosting topological states in different material systems, the stabilization mechanisms behind them, their physical characteristics, and their manipulation by external fields. We then conclude with a perspective on the future trajectory of this rapidly evolving field.

items.title: Editorial: Nano-enabled neural interfaces: transforming brain-machine and neuroprosthetic technologies
items.abstract: For decades, microfabricated silicon probes served as the benchmark for neural recording and they 20 remain the mainstream platforms, although their mechanical mismatch with soft brain tissue can 21 contribute to tissue responses, particularly during long-term implantation. and analyte selectivity in complex biological environments, while event-driven processing must 98 retain information relevant to the intended physiological or behavioural application despite device 99 variability and signal compression. These requirements introduce trade-offs between miniaturisation, 100 measurement fidelity, power consumption and biological compatibility that cannot be resolved 101 through component-level optimisation alone. 102We would like to extend our sincere appreciation and gratitude to the authors, reviewers, and 103 editorial team for their contributions to this Research Topic. We hope this Research Topic will 104 inspire future innovations in nanotechnology and neural interface research. 105

items.title: Charged Three-Dimensional Solitons in a Ferroelectric Nematic Liquid Crystal
items.abstract: Experimental observations and computer simulation of formation and structural properties of so far experimentally never seen electrically charged propagating 3D solitons are reported. The propagating solitons appear spontaneously without an external field in a ferroelectric nematic (NF) liquid crystal under rapid cooling from the antiferroelectric (SmZA) phase. The observed solitons propagate either parallel or antiparallel to the ferroelectric polarization and annihilate when they collide with each other. They are attributed to either positively or negatively charged propagating local polarization splay formed to screen excess negative or positive mobile charge lumps in the NF phase. The presence of mobile charge is attributed to a spatially periodic charge distribution present in the antiferroelectric phase that temporarily remains after the temperature is quenched through the antiferroelectric- ferroelectric phase transition.

items.title: Beyond the European Chips Act: Mobilizing Public Banks to Solve Europe’s Semiconductor Supply Chain Paradox
items.abstract: The European semiconductor supply chain is characterized by a “missing middle.” While the continent hosts global leaders in equipment manufacturing (such as ASML) and advanced research (IMEC, CEA-Leti), its situation in the production of power and automotive semiconductors (STMicroelectronics, Infineon, NXP) has deteriorated, and it is almost entirely absent from the leading edge of logic chip production (with the exception of Intel in Ireland, which produces for the USA). At the same time, Europe is a vast downstream consumer of semiconductors, embedded not only in its automobile, aerospace, and industrial sectors but also in final consumer demand for smartphones, computers, and digital devices. This paradox – strength upstream and downstream, but weakness in the middle of the supply chain – renders the continent acutely vulnerable to economic disruptions and geopolitical shocks. The COVID-19 pandemic exposed these vulnerabilities, as shortages forced months-long shutdowns in European automobile production, while the concentration of advanced-node capacity in Taiwan and South Korea continues to heighten systemic risks. The EU Chips Act (2023) seeks to address this imbalance by doubling Europe’s global market share to 20 percent by 2030. Yet compared with the U.S. CHIPS and Science Act, the initiative remains underfunded and fragmented, with only €3.3 billion in direct EU funding and uneven national subsidies. Intel’s withdrawal from the Magdeburg project has further undermined Europe’s sub-7 nm ambitions. This article argues that Europe requires a more ambitious approach. While direct EU subsidies are off the table due to European institutional constraints, the EU could resort to strategic, highly leveraged, public-private partnerships, where leading players such as TSMC would engage in technology transfer against higher-than-usual profitability. In effect, manufacturers would invest 20% of the total capex needed while public and private banks would provide the remainder. Public promotional banks, such as the EIB, KfW, Bpifrance, CDP, and ICO would be key actors of this plan, because these institutions operate outside the Maastricht definition of public debt, and they could collectively mobilize up to €170 billion between 2026 and 2033.

items.title: Scheduling Data to Compute: Hierarchical Data Pipelining for LLM Training on AMD GPUs
items.abstract: Large language models (LLM) have been the key focus of recent machine learning breakthroughs. As the model size grows exponentially, the computation needed for training is astronomical. A GPU can do a huge amount of arithmetic. However, the data its compute units need is not always available when they are ready. This data may still be in slow memory or on another GPU. While the chip waits, expensive compute sits idle, and at scale even a small drop in utilization translates into substantial cost. In this paper, we treat this waiting time as the primary bottleneck. We focus on hardware features designed for explicit data movement. These features load data from off-chip memory onto the chip, rearrange it into the layout the computation requires as it is loaded, and transfer it between GPUs. By orchestrating them, we keep a steady pipeline of data flowing to the compute units so that they remain busy. We present kernel and framework implementations that address this bottleneck using three key data-movement instructions and hardware features. The Tensor Data Mover (TDM) moves tensor data from high-bandwidth memory (HBM) into on-chip memory. Transpose-load instructions transpose tensor data into the layout that LLM computations require as it is loaded on-chip. Finally, System DMA (SDMA) and Remote DMA (RDMA) move data between GPUs over the scale-up and scale-out networks, respectively. Our results show that TDM and transpose-load provide on average 1.88x and 1.19x speedup at the kernel level, respectively. The SDMA and RDMA lead to on average 1.16x and 1.33x speedup for computation overlapped with communication. This is the first AMD LLM training system to utilize all the GPU data pipelining features. Our implementation has been integrated into open source framework and library for AMD GPUs. https://github.com/AMD-AGI/Primus-Turbo https://github.com/AMD-AGI/Primus

items.title: A Resonant-Tunneling Quantum-Dot Demultiplexer for Scalable Cryogenic Single-Electron Routing
items.abstract: Scaling quantum electronic systems such as quantum-dot spin qubits and single-electron devices is increasingly limited by the wiring overhead between cryogenic devices and room-temperature control electronics. Multi-channel quantum-dot architectures that selectively route electrons using a few shared control lines, analogous to demultiplexers in classical networks, offer a promising solution. Here, we propose and theoretically investigate a gate-defined architecture of three parallel quantum dots sharing a common source reservoir and coupled to independent drain channels. Using an analytical electrostatic model and tight-binding quantum transport simulations, we show that the device can act as an on-chip single-electron demultiplexer based on resonant tunneling in the cryogenic regime. Closed-system eigenstate analysis reveals localized orbital states in each dot, and open-system transport calculations show resonant conductance peaks when these levels align with the incident electron energy, consistent with the closed-system eigenenergy evolution. By engineering the barrier-gate spacing and the relative plunger-gate dimensions, we obtain well-separated resonances with minimal overlap between channels. Bond-current density calculations show that transport is confined to the resonant channel with negligible leakage into neighboring outputs, yielding channel selectivity approaching unity for all resonant modes. The architecture is compatible with Si/SiGe and GaAs/AlGaAs platforms and can be extended to more channels, offering a route toward programmable quantum routing and resonant-tunneling-based quantum circuitry.

items.title: GSPIM: A Temporal-Locality-Aware 4D Gaussian Splatting Accelerator with Polymorphic PIM and Multi-Frame Rendering Dataflow
items.abstract: 4D Gaussian Splatting (4DGS) enables high-quality real-time novel-view synthesis for dynamic scenes, supporting free-viewpoint video, mobile XR, and autonomous systems at the edge. Methods using explicit 4D distributions, keyframe interpolation, or anchor binding share two GPU data-movement bottlenecks. Temporal filtering follows model record loading, wasting LPDDR5 bandwidth on inactive data. Frame-isolated execution also overlooks highly overlapping active sets and depth relationships across adjacent frames, reloading shared attributes when working sets exceed on-chip cache capacity. To address these bottlenecks, we present GSPIM, a temporal-locality-aware 4DGS accelerator for PIM-enabled edge devices. Polymorphic PIM adapts a shared near-memory datapath to representation-specific field layouts and selection procedures. It filters and compacts valid data into contiguous inputs before the GPU accesses complete attributes, reducing ineffective transfers. Multi-Frame Rendering Dataflow reuses active attributes and stable depth relationships within a temporal window, reducing repeated work across frames. Hybrid Dataflow Scheduling overlaps near-memory data preparation with GPU rendering to reduce waiting. Evaluation combines a GPU-PIM model calibrated to Jetson AGX Orin 64 GB with a 1z DRAM physical implementation of the added circuits. Across three 4DGS methods and six dynamic scenes, GSPIM achieves a 4.15x geometric-mean speedup and a 4.99x geometric-mean energy-efficiency improvement over a fully optimized frame-by-frame GPU baseline. The maximum scene-level PSNR difference is 0.011 dB, and the added physical footprint is 18.7172 square millimeters across 32 LPDDR5 dies.

items.title: Memristor‐Based Neuromorphic Computing for Intelligent Sensing and Edge Applications
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Memristor‐based neuromorphic computing has emerged as a promising hardware paradigm for energy‐efficient, scalable artificial intelligence edge applications. This review surveys recent progress in memristor‐based neuromorphic computing, in‐memory computing architectures, learning algorithms, and hardware implementations for edge intelligence. Volatile and nonvolatile memristive dynamics are discussed as key mechanisms for emulating biological neurons and synapses, providing foundational building blocks for crossbar‐based hardware neural networks. Moving beyond conventional neural‐network acceleration, this review examines the integration of memristive technologies into edge‐specific applications, focusing on emerging in‐sensor computing, optical in‐memory computing, and multimodal sensing frameworks. Furthermore, we outline the deployment of hardware‐compatible, brain‐inspired algorithms—including artificial, spiking, and recurrent neural networks—and evaluate their physical implementation within memristive architectures. The review also highlights the evolution of memristor‐based hardware from single‐device demonstrations to array‐level accelerators and CMOS‐integrated system‐on‐chip platforms, with the associated hierarchical challenges and solutions. By bridging the gap between individual device physics and full system engineering, this review provides a comprehensive roadmap for developing highly adaptive, low‐latency, and autonomous hardware platforms for the next generation of localized edge intelligence.

items.title: In-Memory Computing Architectures for Accelerating Large-Scale Models: Principles, Devices, and System Challenges
items.abstract: Memory bandwidth is the binding constraint for large-model inference today. In-memory computing (IMC) addresses this limitation. This paper reviews where the technology stands. It compares analog and digital IMC implementations and find that analog arrays currently lead on energy efficiency, while digital designs maintain a substantial edge in precision and programming flexibility. Then it discusses three device candidates: Resistive Random-Access Memory (ReRAM), Ferroelectric Field-Effect Transistor (FeFET), and Spin-Transfer-Torque Magnetic Random-Access Memory (STT-MRAM). ReRAM offers the highest density but suffers from stochastic filament growth and conductance drift. FeFETs integrate cleanly with CMOS but are limited by ferroelectric switching variability. STT-MRAM is the most durable and stable, yet its modest tunnel-magnetoresistance ratio restricts analog precision. Finally, three limitations are pointed out: device variation under realistic workloads, peripheral-circuit overhead that can erase array-level energy gains, and scalable multi-chip orchestration for trillion-parameter models. IMC will succeed or fail based on cross-layer co-design—not on any single device breakthrough. Materials, circuits, compilers, and algorithms must advance together, and the compiler layer remains underdeveloped relative to device research. This paper provides development ideas for higher performance for IMC.

items.title: Hump modulation in Transfer Characteristics: Simulated Gate-all-around field-effect transistors — Supporting TCAD Simulation Data
items.abstract: A parasitic current path beneath the bottom nanosheet of a simulated triple-stacked silicon gate-all-around field-effect transistor (GAA-FET) accompanies a hump in the low-drain-bias transfer curve. In a separate punch-through stopper (PTS) simulation, both the hump and the drive current were reduced, indicating a substrate-side contribution. Without altering the substrate structure, the hump is also dependent on channel and source/drain conditions throughout 486 parameter combinations. For channel widths of 8 and 12 nm, the mean peak-to-valley logarithmic-current gradient difference was lower by 51.2% in the wider-channel case. At 0.05 V drain bias and 8 nm channel width, the interface trap density was changed from 1010 to 1012 cm-2 eV-1. Hump onset moved to more positive gate voltage for all 27 paired conditions, with a mean shift of 23.91 ± 0.49 mV. The change in gradient difference has a coefficient of variation (CV) of 24.3%. The onset shift has a CV of 2.1%. Different relative contributions from nanosheet and substrate currents can account for these responses. Channel and source/drain parameters may thus modify hump shape without additional substrate-isolation structures.

items.title: High-performance annealing-free wurtzite ferroelectric field-effect transistors with ultrathin oxide semiconductors for neuromorphic computing
items.abstract: Wurtzite-structured aluminum scandium nitride (AlScN) ferroelectric materials are potential candidates for non-volatile memory (NVM) applications because of their high remanent polarization (Pr > 100 μC·cm−2) and compatibility with back-end-of-line (BEOL) processes. However, achieving high-performance wurtzite ferroelectric field-effect transistors (FeFETs) remains a significant challenge because of their high interface trap density (Dit) and large threshold voltage (VTH) variation. Here we show the distinct polarization switching mechanisms of AlScN FeFETs based on an ultrathin indium gallium oxide (IGO) channel with three different structures. FeFETs with a metal–ferroelectric–metal–insulator–semiconductor (MFMIS) structure show high interface quality with low Dit and a stable VTH, achieving a large memory window (MW) of up to 20.6 V and a high endurance of 106. The stable 6-bit operation of our devices with 64 distinct states shows the feasibility of multilevel storage applications. Furthermore, we demonstrate the applicability of the FeFET in neuromorphic networks, with a high recognition accuracy of 93.02%. AlScN field-effect transistors for non-volatile memory are limited by high interface trap density and threshold voltage instability. Wang et al. demonstrate annealing-free AlScN ferroelectric transistors with low interface trap density and stable threshold voltage, enabling a large memory window and robust 6-bit operation.

items.title: Advanced Capacitor and Supercapacitor Structures Based on Functional Thin Films
items.abstract: Thin-film capacitors and supercapacitors are gaining increasing attention due to the rapid development of modern electronics, flexible devices, microsystems and wearable technologies. Their small size, low weight and compatibility with integrated electronic systems make them promising components for next-generation applications and energy-storage systems. In recent years, significant progress has been achieved in the development of thin-film structures with improved capacitance, higher energy density, lower leakage current and better thermal and electrical stability. Advances in thin-film engineering have also enabled the use of high-k dielectric materials, ultrathin insulating layers, oxide-based electrodes and advanced carbon materials to enhance device performance. This review presents recent progress in thin-film capacitor and supercapacitor technologies, focusing on device architectures, dielectric and electrode thin films and reliability-related challenges. Different configurations, including metal–insulator–metal (MIM), metal–oxide–semiconductor (MOS), interdigital, flexible and three-dimensional structures, are discussed. Special attention is given to oxide thin films, nanostructured electrodes, interface quality, defect-related phenomena and scaling effects influencing electrical performance. Current market trends and commercial perspectives are also discussed in the context of emerging electronic applications. Finally, key technological challenges and future development directions for thin-film capacitors and supercapacitors are highlighted.

items.title: qLevelPlace: A Level-Based Placement Framework for RSFQ Circuits
items.abstract: Rapid Single Flux Quantum (RSFQ) logic can operate at ultra-high clock frequencies; however, its physical design is complicated by explicit splitter trees and deep gate-level pipelines in which every logic gate is clocked. To address this challenge, we present qLevelPlace, a level-based placement framework for RSFQ circuits. We separate gate and splitter placement into two stages to better support levelguided gate-to-row assignment and use a timing-aware quadratic cost function to penalize long interconnects. Experiments on the benchmark circuits show that, on average, qLevelPlace achieves a $2.65\times$ higher clock frequency and a 51% reduction in layout area compared with the state-of-the-art RSFQ placer qPlace.

items.title: PagedMoE: Cross-Precision Expert Caching for Token-Level Dynamic Precision in SSD-Resident MoE Inference
items.abstract: Large Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models are promising for local inference because sparse routing allows the routed-expert pool to reside on SSD while DRAM caches recently used experts. However, under practical DRAM cache capacities, substantial SSD I/O remains on the critical path despite I/O-computation overlap. Token-level dynamic expert precision offers a natural way to reduce this data demand by allocating bits according to expert importance and quantization sensitivity. Nevertheless, treating each bit-width of the same expert as an independent object prevents cross-precision cache reuse, causing overlapping data to be fetched repeatedly. The key insight is that precision should instead denote the refinement depth of one shared expert state. Based on this insight, we present PagedMoE, which stores each expert once using a prefix-compatible tree codebook and bitplane layout. Lower-precision representations are valid prefixes of higher-precision ones, allowing cached data to be reused or extended by fetching only missing bitplanes. PagedMoE selects the required prefix length before I/O using current routing weights and offline expert-specific error profiles, and directly executes cached 1-8-bit prefixes without materializing full-precision experts. At an average routed-expert precision of 2.5 bits, PagedMoE achieves quality close to GPTQ-INT4 on Qwen3.5-397B-A17B and to MXFP4 on most evaluated GLM5.2 tasks. With a 24 GiB expert cache, it reaches 8.89 tokens/s on Qwen3.5, 1.33x the throughput of the same dynamic requests using independent precision objects and 1.56x that of uniform 4-bit execution.

items.title: Continuous Kinetic Model of Counterion-Mediated Redox Switching in 14-Bit Molecular Memristors for Analog In-Memory Computing
items.abstract: Kinetic molecular memristors offer a compelling path toward high-density analog in-memory computing by achieving 14-bit precision, wherein discrete redox transitions and counterion displacements dictate non-volatile conductance across a deterministic energy landscape. However, integrating these nanoscale kinetics into macroscale circuit simulators has remained bottlenecked by derivative discontinuities and solver convergence failures. Here, we present a physics-inspired continuous kinetic model that bridges microscopic molecular transport with scalable circuit architectures. By casting discrete intramolecular states, counterion relaxation dynamics, and Marcus-Hush-Chidsey electron transfer rates into continuously differentiable state variables, we derive a robust, Spectre-compatible compact model and a matching vectorized Python solver. This work culminates in a unified computational platform to reliably predict the behavior of complex circuits built on these molecular memristors.

items.title: Accelerating LLM Decoding with In-DRAM Parallelism
items.abstract: Autoregressive decoding of large language models (LLMs) on edge devices is dominated by memory-bound general matrix--vector multiplication (GeMV) operations. Processing-using-DRAM (PUD) is a promising computing paradigm that can alleviate this bottleneck by reducing processor--memory data transfers and enabling massively parallel computation within DRAM (e.g., across 65,536 columns). However, weight matrices in individual LLM layers (e.g., a QKV matrix in Llama3 8B with 6,144 rows) are typically too small to fully utilize parallelism in PUD. To address this challenge, we propose an algorithm--system co-design for PUD-based LLM inference. At the algorithm level, we enable a subsequent projection to be packed with the current projection by reformulating it as a computation on the current residual state plus a correction for the residual update. Layer redundancy allows this correction to be approximated using fewer bit-serial steps. At the system level, we tailor data mapping and execution to improve utilization of either columns within DRAM subarrays (SIMD) or independently controlled banks (MIMD). Overall, we achieves up to $1.41\times$ end-to-end decoding speedup over the PUD baseline, corresponding to a $2.45\times$ speedup over processor-based execution.

items.title: Universal model of the growth of III-V tetrahedral semiconductors on polar surfaces: pyramids and glue atoms. VI. Surface diffusion on a nonmetal-terminated surface
items.abstract: Ab initio calculations were used to simulate surface diffusion of adsorbates on the nonmetal-terminated surface of tetrahedral semiconductors: GaN, GaP, GaAs and GaSb. These surfaces are wurtzite gallium nitride, i.e. GaN(000-1) surface, zinc blende gallium phosphide, i.e. GaP(-1-1-1) gallium arsenide, GaAs (-1-1-1) and gallium antimonide GaSb (-1-1-1) surfaces. The mixed coverage consists of Ga adatoms in the first layer with a nonmetal atom attached above them forming a triangular-based pyramid. The pyramidal structures are stable during surface jumps involving rotations around one of the basal Ga adatoms. Thus, the diffusion proceeds via rotation (pivot) of the pair of the other basal Ga adatoms around an immobile Ga adatom moving them into new, originally empty sites. Using an energy-path determination procedure, the diffusion barriers were obtained as the difference between the initial site energy and the activated complex state energy. The detachment energy of the NM adatom was obtained assuming a final state in atomic and molecular form. The energy barrier for detachment to the atomic state is high for all atoms, on the order of 5 eV. For the molecular state these barriers are different: smaller for nitrogen, on the order of 1 eV, which is related to the high dissociation energy of the N2 molecule. For P and As the barrier is above 2 eV. For Sb it was not determined. Accordingly, the surface diffusion length is macroscopically large, indicating that all NM adatoms arrive at the steps.

items.title: Temperature-Independent Logarithmic Current Slope in Interdiffusion-Broadened Silicon pn Junction toward Low-Power Thermometry
items.abstract: With the development of cryogenic technologies such as quantum computing, there is an increasing need for low-power cryogenic thermometers that minimize self-heating. Here, we report an anomalous temperature-independent logarithmic current slope, $d(\ln J)/dV$, in heavily doped silicon p$^{+}$n$^{+}$ junctions with significant dopant interdiffusion and highlight the advantages of our device as a low-power, cryogenic thermometer. Electrical characterizations from 2 to 420 K reveal that, at low forward bias, $d(\ln J)/dV$ remains nearly constant, which yields a voltage-temperature responsivity that is nearly independent of bias current. The observed transport cannot be fully understood with conventional diffusion or direct band-to-band tunneling. Instead, the results suggest the contribution of trap-assisted tunneling. These results establish interdiffusion-broadened silicon p$^{+}$n$^{+}$ junctions as a route to low-power temperature sensors while providing insight into carrier transport in heavily doped semiconductor junctions.

items.title: Technical Challenges for Ultra Fine Pitch Hybrid Bonding
items.abstract: Hybrid bonding is rapidly emerging as a foundational technology for next-generation advanced packaging, enabling ultra-high-density interconnects required for heterogeneous integration of chiplets, logic, memory, and specialized accelerators. As the industry pushes toward ultra-fine pitch interconnects approaching single-digit microns and below, significant technical challenges must be addressed across the process flow. These challenges include achieving extremely tight wafer and die alignment tolerances, maintaining surface planarity and cleanliness at the nanometer scale, controlling copper dishing and dielectric erosion during CMP, and ensuring defect-free oxide and copper-copper bonding interfaces. In addition, scaling hybrid bonding to ultra-fine pitch requires improvements in metrology, defect inspection, thermal management, and yield control to support high-volume manufacturing. Integration with complementary technologies such as silicon interposers, wafer-to-wafer and die-to-wafer bonding architectures, and heterogeneous material stacks further increases process complexity. This presentation reviews the key technical barriers to ultra-fine pitch hybrid bonding and discusses emerging process solutions and equipment innovations required to enable reliable, high-density interconnects for future high-performance computing, AI, and advanced system-in-package applications.

items.title: TD-MSEFormer: temporal dependency multi-scale expert former for IGBT remaining useful life prediction
items.abstract: Accurate remaining useful life (RUL) prediction of insulated gate bipolar transistors (IGBTs) is important for ensuring the reliability of power electronic systems. However, IGBT degradation sequences usually exhibit nonlinear evolution, mixed short-term and long-term dependencies, and stage-dependent degradation characteristics, which makes robust RUL prediction challenging. To address these issues, this paper proposes a Temporal Dependency Multi-Scale Expert Former (TD-MSEFormer). Specifically, a Sequential Dependency Calibration Module (SDCM) is introduced to enhance degradation-related temporal dependency representation. A Multi-Scale Temporal Expert Block (MSTEB) is designed to capture degradation patterns at different temporal scales, while a Temporal Dual-Attention (TDA) block further refines local temporal interactions. Extensive experiments on NASA IGBT Aging Dataset demonstrate that the proposed TD-MSEFormer consistently outperforms other methods, achieving the best overall RUL prediction performance with superior accuracy, robust generalization, and stable degradation representation under complex nonlinear aging conditions.

items.title: Scalable p-type Te 1-x Se x thin-film transistors and low-power complementary logic gates
items.abstract: Abstract Despite the promise of Te as a p-type channel material, realizing Te-based thin-film transistors (TFTs) with low off-state current and high on/off ratio is challenging due to its small bandgap and high background carrier density. Se-alloying offers a potential solution to mitigate these limitations, yet the device performance has remained suboptimal. In this work, through the synergy of stoichiometric control and thickness engineering, we achieve an optimal trade-off between charge transport and switching characteristics in Te1-xSex TFTs. The resulting devices exhibit an average field-effect mobility of 16.8 cm2 V-1 s-1, Ion/Ioff ratio of 1.3×105 and an ultralow off-state current of 10 pA μm-1. The fabrication process is fully compatible with established low-temperature TFT technologies, enabling high-yield production of transistor arrays with favorable electrical uniformity. Notably, the devices demonstrate exceptional environmental stability, retaining critical performance metrics after six months of storage without encapsulation. Complementary logic gates (NOT, NAND, and NOR) are fabricated by integrating p-Te0.63Se0.37 and n-IGZO TFTs. The inverter achieves a high voltage gain of 28, a noise margin of 92.3%, and a low static power consumption of 420 pW at 3 V supply voltage. This study highlights the potential of Te1-xSex as a scalable p-type channel material, advancing the development of TFT-based logic circuits.

items.title: Robust Power-Law Computing for Edge Intelligence Using Spin-Orbit Torque Magnetic Tunnel Junctions
items.abstract: Power-law transformations are widely used in edge perception, where compact implementations must balance numerical precision, circuit resources, and device variability. Here we demonstrate a stochastic power-law architecture based on spin-orbit-torque magnetic tunnel junctions (SOT-MTJs). An event-driven feedback loop adjusts the write voltage to regulate the probability of an all-1 event in an n-bit block. Under the fixed-point sampling model, this establishes a switching probability p=b1/n, from which m-bit event statistics yield the power-law target bm/n. Online probability locking removes the need for offline per-device probability-voltage characterization or stored calibration tables. Measurements on W-based SOT-MTJs, combined with digital analysis of the acquired bitstreams, demonstrate representative power-law operations with absolute deviations of 0.003 or less at the reported precision, as well as parallel decoding of multiple exponents from one source. A 4-bit gamma-correction example preserves dark-region image detail and reaches approximately 35 dB peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) relative to the theoretical gamma-domain reference near 1000 raw samples. A 5 Oe device-level field perturbation and a joint {plus minus}90% simulation centered on the measured parameter means of 25 devices examine adaptation and the safe-voltage operating boundary under the tested conditions. These results establish a nonlinear computing primitive with accuracy controlled by sampling depth and an operating point maintained through feedback.

items.title: Physics-aware calibration neural network for automated TCAD-to-experiment modeling of carbon nanotube field-effect transistors
items.abstract: Abstract Low-dimensional semiconductor devices, including carbon nanotube field-effect transistors (CNT-FETs), require efficient calibration methods to reconcile numerical simulations with experimentally measured electrical characteristics. Conventional manual calibration is time-consuming, while purely data-driven surrogate models may provide limited physical interpretability and reduced reliability when applied to device geometries outside the training domain. In this work, we propose a physics-aware calibration neural network (PACNN) for supervised technology computer-aided design (TCAD)-to-experiment calibration of CNT-FET transfer and output characteristics. PACNN uses current–voltage curves generated by a two-dimensional intrinsic silicon TCAD model as a stable numerical reference. The architecture combines an anchor-preserving physical-affine module, which accounts for global variations in voltage alignment, current amplitude, slope, and extracted electrical parameters, with family-specific bounded residual modules that correct the remaining local discrepancies. Transfer characteristics are processed in the signed logarithmic current domain, whereas output characteristics are calibrated in the normalized linear current domain using separate amplitude and low-rank shape corrections. Model training incorporates curve-fitting, curve-level R 2 , slope consistency, device parameter, residual, and regularization objectives. Channel-length generalization was evaluated through out-of-distribution (OOD) extrapolation to $${L}_\mathrm{ch}$$ L ch = 4.5 μm and 5.0 μm. PACNN achieved macro-averaged curve-wise R 2 values of 0.947 4 and 0.876 0 for the transfer and output characteristics, respectively, with corresponding pooled pointwise R 2 values of 0.962 7 and 0.996 2. The predicted curves also preserved key electrical parameters, yielding a balanced physical consistency index of 0.918 3. These results indicate that PACNN provides an accurate and physically constrained framework for automated TCAD-to-experiment calibration of CNT-FET characteristics.

items.title: PRISM: Unifying multiphysics optothermal transport and identifiability-guided inference for nanoscale thermal metrology
items.abstract: Quantifying thermal transport across micro- and nanoscale heterostructures is critical for solid-state devices and relies on fitting heat-transfer models to thermal-wave spectra. When probing scales approach optical absorption depths, electron-phonon equilibration lengths, or phonon mean free paths, classical surface-heating Fourier models can match measured phase spectra while returning biased, measurement-dependent parameters. Here we introduce PRISM (Physics-Resolved Inference and Screening Meta-framework), an agentic framework coupling multilayer optical transfer-matrix electrodynamics, two-temperature electron-phonon relaxation, and nonlocal Guyer-Krumhansl phonon hydrodynamics within a unified admittance formalism, paired with singular-value-decomposition identifiability screening and knowledge-guided routing. Demonstrated with frequency-domain thermoreflectance across stacks relevant to microelectronic contacts and dielectric barriers, PRISM corrects a 24-28% interfacial conductance underestimation in Au/Si, recovers intrinsic silica conductivity in Au/Ti/SiO$_2$, and eliminates a 40% cross-plane conductivity underestimation in Au/MoS$_2$. In bimetallic Au/Ti/Si stacks, where all three non-classical mechanisms act simultaneously, nonlocal modeling reconciles the $116$-$137$ W m$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$ local-fit scatter across spot sizes and frequency windows into a configuration-independent intrinsic silicon conductivity of $141$ W m$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$. For ion-irradiated and graded media with continuous conductivity profiles, PRISM can autonomously construct and verify a deep operator network solver to reconstruct steep damage gradients. By uniting non-equilibrium transport physics and identifiability screening with autonomous model synthesis, PRISM establishes a generalizable paradigm readily extensible to broader optothermal and thermal-wave metrology modalities.

items.title: Multifunctional spin-valley-topological transport and magneto-optical responses in Janus bimetallic CrMnCF2 monolayer
items.abstract: Two-dimensional Janus magnetic materials provide a platform for coupled spin, valley, and magneto-optical phenomena due to broken inversion symmetry. Here we investigate a Janus CrMnCF 2 monolayer using first-principles calculations and Monte Carlo simulations. The calculated results support the thermodynamic, dynamical, and mechanical stability of the CrMnCF 2 monolayer. It exhibits a ferromagnetic ground state with out-of-plane magnetic anisotropy, where Cr and Mn 3 d states dominate the magnetism and induce strong exchange-driven spin splitting. Including spin–orbit coupling, structural asymmetry and ferromagnetism lift the K/K′ valley degeneracy, producing a robust valley splitting of ∼33 meV under biaxial strain (−5% to +5%). Opposite Berry curvature at the two valleys leads to valley-dependent transport and a sizable intrinsic anomalous Hall conductivity of about −130 S/cm under hole doping. In addition, the system exhibits an intrinsic magneto-optical Kerr effect without an external magnetic field, with a maximum Kerr rotation of approximately 130 mdeg in the ultraviolet region. These results highlight CrMnCF 2 as a multifunctional 2D material for spintronic, valleytronic, and magneto-optical applications.

items.title: Modeling and Analysis of Reliability Challenges in Nanoscale Transistors
items.abstract: To meet the speed, complexity, circuit density, power consumption, and ultimately cost requirements of many advanced applications, scientists have spent decades shrinking device feature sizes for better performance of metal-oxide semiconductor (MOS) technology. However, there are several disadvantages to switching to these nano size MOS devices. Most of the functional failure in nano-scale devices is caused by aging related phenomena such as negative bias temperature instability (NBTI), hot carrier degradation (HCD), and time dependent dielectric breakdown (TDDB). However, Silicon devices’ dimensions and material capabilities are beginning to hit their limitations. Scientists and researchers have figured out how to replace the current silicon material with an emerging novel material like carbon nano tube. The goal of this research was to develop a drain current and threshold voltage model for carbon nanotube field effect transistors (CNTFETs) that can be used in the analysis and design of reliable integrated circuits, focusing on the reliability issues of conventional metal oxide semiconductor field-effect transistors (MOSFETs) at the nanoscale. To develop this model, we investigated the atomic structure of carbon nanotubes and used the fundamentals of electrostatics to describe a field-effect transistor. By analyzing and defining the electronic structure of carbon nanotubes, we first arrived at analytical formulas for the carrier concentration in carbon nanotubes for various chiral vectors (n, m). By combining several chiral vectors, it is possible to determine the threshold voltage expression that is obtained throughout the procedure as well as the I-V characteristics for CNTFETs. The diameter and chiral angle of carbon nanotubes were shown to be significant determinants of the I-V characteristics and threshold voltage. In terms of the threshold voltage change CNTFET shows better performance 24% less than the conventional MOSFET in 45nm technology node.
items.venue: Saudi Journal of Engineering and Technology

items.title: Methodology for determining interface-state density in AlGaN/GaN MIS-HEMT structures using sub-bandgap illumination
items.abstract: In this work, we present a methodology for determining the interface-state density distribution in metal-insulator-semiconductor (MIS) AlGaN/GaN heterostructures using sub-bandgap illumination. First, we discuss the electronic transitions that occur during sub-bandgap illumination of MIS AlGaN/GaN heterostructures. In particular, we show how these transitions can induce a threshold-voltage shift in MIS AlGaN/GaN HEMT structures and, consequently, lead to a completely erroneous interpretation of the results. In this context, we experimentally demonstrate that the interface-state density distribution can be significantly overestimated due to, for example, free-hole generation resulting from electronic transitions via interface states at the AlGaN/insulator interface and/or deep levels in the GaN buffer layer. Finally, we provide guidelines for the accurate determination of the interface-state density in MIS AlGaN/GaN heterostructures using sub-bandgap illumination, including detailed measurement and analysis procedures.

items.title: Memristor-Based In-Memory Computing for Artificial Intelligence Acceleration: A Review of Devices, Crossbar Architectures, Benefits and Challenges
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence workloads are dominated by multiply-and-accumulate operations on very large weight matrices. In conventional processors these weights must be moved repeatedly between memory and the arithmetic units, and this data movement, rather than the arithmetic itself, consumes most of the energy and time. Memristor-based in-memory computing (IMC) addresses this limitation by performing computation inside the memory array. A memristor is a two-terminal resistive switching device whose conductance can be programmed and retained, so it can store a weight. When memristors are arranged in a crossbar, Ohm's law and Kirchhoff's current law cause the column currents to equal the product of an input voltage vector and the conductance matrix, so a complete vector–matrix multiplication is obtained in a single analog step. This review explains the memristor concept and its physical realisations, the working principle of crossbar arrays, and the peripheral circuits and system architecture needed to build an accelerator. Representative device-level and system-level studies are compared. The benefits for AI inference and training are assessed against non-idealities such as device variability, limited precision, conductance drift, wire resistance and the cost of analog-to-digital conversion. Applications and research directions are identified.
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

items.title: Material optimization of interconnects and transistors for energy-efficient and high-performance cryogenic GAA technology
items.abstract: Abstract Unprecedented computational demand is reshaping the landscape of energy-efficient and high-performance computing. As Moore’s law approaches its physical limits, continued progress to meet this demand can no longer rely solely on transistor scaling. Cryogenic operation of CMOS circuits offers a promising path forward, enhancing the subthreshold slope (SS) of transistors while enabling certain materials to exhibit superconductivity. This dual advantage positions device- and material-level optimizations as a compelling solution for next-generation cryogenic computing. In this work, we demonstrate that unlocking the full potential of cryogenic CMOS requires strategic transistor and interconnect-level optimizations. We show that (1) material optimization for tuning transistor work function is vital for translating SS improvements into a significant increase in ON current, while (2) exploiting superconducting interconnect materials at cryogenic temperatures is essential to eliminate resistive parasitics and overcome interconnect bottlenecks. To quantify these benefits, we employ a cryogenic-aware 2 nm gate-all-around nanosheet digital design flow, incorporating calibrated device models along with a full standard cell library. Our evaluation results targeting the compute fabric of the AI accelerator circuit demonstrate that our optimizations provide a 3× increase in TOPS, 7.7× increase in TOPS/W, and 23× improvement in efficiency TOPS 2 /W.

items.title: Laser-transferrable GaN HEMTs based on high-quality AlN/GaN/AlN sacrificing templates
items.abstract: Laser lift-off (LLO) technology is an effective approach to fabricate transferrable GaN high-electron-mobility transistors (HEMTs) and address self-heating effects during device operation. However, conventional approaches struggle with precise control of LLO positions and structural integrity of devices, especially for those with AlN-based back barriers (BBs). Herein, we develop a laser-transferrable GaN HEMT with a μm-scale AlN BB, which is grown on a novel template including a GaN sacrificing layer (SL) and a metalorganic chemical vapor deposition-grown AlN nucleation layer (MO-AlN NL). The MO-AlN serves as the dislocation filtering layer to suppress dislocation propagation in the GaN SL, thereby creating an optimized nucleation template for the AlN BB. As such, the AlN-on-GaN epitaxy proceeds in a coherent 2D growth mode with largely reduced threading dislocations and preserved compressive strain. The devices fabricated on this AlN-BB/GaN-SL/AlN-NL tri-layer template can be integrally detached by a 266-nm UV laser, which only breaks the GaN SL and leaves an intact device active region. This work simultaneously resolves the critical challenges in μm-scale AlN-on-GaN epitaxy and laser transfer of GaN HEMTs with AlN-based BBs, offering a viable approach to laser-transferrable GaN power/RF devices with customized device structures toward improved device characteristics and thermal management.

items.title: High-Performance GaN HEMTs on an Ultrathin 4H-SiC/Diamond Engineered Substrate via Optimized Epitaxial Growth
items.abstract: Abstract GaN high-electron-mobility transistors (HEMTs) were fabricated on an ultrathin 4H-SiC/diamond engineered substrate using an optimized epitaxial growth scheme. Optimization of the epitaxial growth conditions improved epitaxial quality and carrier transport properties.The fabricated devices exhibited a maximum DC drain current density of approximately 1.25 A/mm and a peak transconductance of 367 mS/mm, demonstrating high current capability on the engineered substrate platform. Infrared thermography yielded a low-power thermal resistance of 0.92 K•mm/W, compared with 2.46 K•mm/W for a GaN-on-SiC reference device.The device on the engineered substrate sustained a maximum DC power dissipation density of 37.8 W/mm. These results demonstrate the potential of the optimized GaN-on-4H-SiC/diamond platform for high-performance GaN devices with enhanced thermal management.

items.title: Distributed Charge-Trap Dynamics in Graphene Transistors Revealed by RF Impedance Dispersion
items.abstract: Abstract Charge trapping at the graphene/dielectric interface is a major source of instability in graphene transistors, yet its signature in the radio-frequency electrical response remains poorly understood and characterized. This work reports that trap-related charge exchange along the graphene channel produces a distinct, frequency-dependent dispersion in the transistor output impedance, observable from standard microwave measurements without dedicated stress or pulsed-bias protocols. This dispersion primarily affects the reactive part of the output impedance, particularly at low frequencies, and gradually diminishes toward the GHz range, consistent with a distribution of trap relaxation times along the channel. To capture this behavior, a non-uniform transmission-line model is developed that treats channel trapping as a spatially distributed process. An equivalent lumped circuit, consisting of a single RC branch in parallel with the channel resistance, reproduces the distributed response accurately, and explicit analytic relationships between both representations enable extraction of local distributed-model parameters from the lumped circuit. The equivalent capacitance converges to a stable value as the number of distributed trapping sections increases, whereas the effective time constant remains dependent on trap position, preserving information about the distributed nature of the phenomenon. Using the converged values, the extracted interfacial trap density is consistent with reported values for graphene/AlOx interfaces, and the extracted trap dynamics depend systematically on channel aspect ratio, identifying device geometry as a means of tuning the frequency range over which trap-induced dispersion is observable. Excellent agreement between model and experimental data is demonstrated across the full characterization frequency range, and the resulting trap-aware description further improves prediction of the device input reflection coefficient. This work establishes high-frequency electrical characterization, interpreted through a distributed-to-lumped framework, as a non-destructive, quantitative route to probe the density, spatial distribution, and dynamics of traps in graphene channels, with direct relevance to interface engineering and defect characterization of graphene devices.

items.title: Challenges and Opportunities in 2D Materials: An Indian Perspective
items.abstract: Abstract Two-dimensional (2D) materials (Graphene, 2D transition metal dichalcogenides (MX 2 ), hBN) have emerged as exciting materials for discovering novel physical phenomena, and have great potential for electronic and optoelectronic devices, as well as energy and catalysis applications. Further, materials such as Cr 2 X 2 Te 6 (X = Si, Ge), VSe 2 , Fe 3 GeTe 2 , CrX 3 (X = Cl, Br, I) and MPX 3 (M = Mn, Fe, V, Zn, Co, Ni, Cd, Mg; X = S, Se) have emerged as fascinating platforms for 2D magnetism. The heterostructures of these 2D materials, and the twist angle between layers are opening new possibilities of studying the effect of Moiré potential, exotic topological phases, magnetic-proximity effects, and strong correlations. At the same time, the research is leading towards many application-based directions such as in excitonics, valleytronics, straintronics, and quantum technologies. In this context, growth of novel 2D materials and heterostructures, as well as large scale growth becomes critically important. This roadmap aims to provide a comprehensive overview of 2D materials research in India and across the globe. The roadmap is broadly divided into six themes: 1. Topology in 2D Materials, Magnetism, Exotic Physics and Emergent Phenomena; 2. Moiré Physics in 2D Heterostructures; 3. Excitonic Physics and Optical properties, including Defects; 4. Transport Phenomena in 2D Materials; 5. 2D Materials Synthesis and Growth; and 6. 2D Materials Electrical Devices and Applications. This roadmap highlights the cutting edge-research being done by Indian and global researchers, emphasizes the challenges, and suggests possible technological solutions.

items.title: SMART-AIMC: Sensitivity-Aware Mixed ADC Resolution with Fine-Grained Tunability for Analog In-Memory Computing
items.abstract: Analog In-Memory Computing (IMC) is a promising paradigm for accelerating GEMM-based AI workloads by executing computations directly within the memory array in the analog domain. While IMC delivers substantial energy and throughput improvements, it can suffer from significant task accuracy degradation due to analog-to-digital converter (ADC) quantization noise, which occurs at the GEMM output and is thus different from weight/activation quantization, which occurs at the GEMM input. Mixed ADC resolution allows IMC modules to choose between high- and low-resolution ADC modes with different energy costs, offering a compelling accuracy-energy trade-off. However, selecting ADC resolutions across IMC units while respecting hardware granularity constraints remains challenging. In this paper, we propose SMART-AIMC, a Sensitivity-aware Mixed ADC Resolution framework with fine-grained Tunability for Analog In-Memory Computing. SMART-AIMC correlates the algorithmic task loss to hardware ADC quantization noise in the form of an ADC Channel Sensitivity (ACS) metric. Using this metric, SMART-AIMC systematically, and in a disciplined manner, allocates ADC resources to critical computations. Furthermore, we introduce a sensitivity-based channel reordering scheme that overcomes the hardware granularity constraints with no runtime overhead and approaches the optimal ADC quantization possible for the model. Evaluated across diverse workloads, SMART-AIMC unlocks a superior accuracy-energy Pareto frontier, providing (1) higher task accuracy at matched energy budgets and (2) fine-grained tuning across efficiency targets, from aggressive energy savings to near-digital inference accuracy. At the latter operating point, SMART-AIMC achieves $6.99\times$ higher modeled system-level energy efficiency for linear projections than the INT8 digital baseline with negligible accuracy degradation.

items.title: A Surrogate Model for Variation-Aware Clock-Mesh Analysis and Design-Space Exploration using Graph Neural Networks
items.abstract: Clock meshes are widely used in high-performance VLSI systems to minimize skew and tolerate On-Chip Variation (OCV) in nanometer technologies. However, analyzing meshes is difficult because reconvergent paths and multi-source drivers prevent static timing analysis (STA) tools from handling mesh loops, making SPICE the industrial standard. SPICE simulations are accurate but slow, so clock-mesh synthesis relies on approximate models that overlook critical effects such as non-linear buffer driving caused by input slew and input skew. We propose a Graph Neural Network (GNN) based surrogate model of the clock mesh with a new graph representation and a new architecture that predicts power while also improving the delay and slew predictions at the sinks and capturing the skew histogram under OCV. Trained on SPICE data and tested on unseen real designs, our model achieves average errors of $3.40$~ps in delay, $4.14$~ps in slew and $4.46$~ps in skew, compared with $6.28$~ps, $12.35$~ps, and $11.62$~ps for our prior model, and $74.37$~ps delay and $27.51$~ps skew for the approximate method used in current state-of-the-art works. Our model predicts power within $3.4\%$ of SPICE on average, while delivering $18\times$-$1706\times$ speed-ups over the approximate method under OCV modeling, enabling faster and more accurate clock-mesh design-space exploration. A case study on a real design further shows that our surrogate model finds buffering candidates that, at a balanced tradeoff, improves $99^{\text{th}}$-percentile skew by $49.1\%$, reduces power by $25.7\%$, and reduces area by $37.3\%$ at the cost of a $6.8\%$ increase in $99^{\text{th}}$-percentile maximum slew as compared to the state-of-the-art work.

items.title: Threshold voltage instability in Schottky p-GaN gate HEMTs under dynamic gate stress
items.abstract: This work investigates the threshold voltage instability of 650-V Schottky p-GaN gate HEMTs under dynamic gate stress (DGS). The effects of gate bias, temperature, switching frequency, and duty cycle on the threshold voltage shift (ΔV TH ) are experimentally analyzed. The results show that ΔV TH strongly depends on the applied stress conditions and arises from the interplay of multiple charge-trapping mechanisms within the gate stack. In particular, increasing gate bias enhances the negative threshold voltage shift, while higher temperature and switching frequency promote positive contributions that partially compensate for the negative drift. Duty cycle is also found to play a key role by modifying the effective positive-bias time and the balance between competing trapping mechanisms. A comparison with DC constant-voltage stress further highlights the importance of dynamic stress conditions in determining the threshold-voltage evolution. These findings provide further insight into the reliability behavior of p-GaN HEMTs under DGS conditions relevant to switching operation.

items.title: Roll-to-Roll fabrication Cu-Carbon Nanotube composites for advanced electrical conductors
items.abstract: We report on the development of high-volume, continuous-feed, roll-to-roll (R2R) batch-processing capability for the scalable fabrication (>1 m length) of high-performance composite conductors that incorporate carbon nanotubes (CNTs) into the Cu matrix, ultra-conductive metal composites (UCC). Long-length UCCs are formed by uniformly coating Cu tapes with aligned CNT-infused polymer nanofibers via an electrospinning unit followed by R2R thermal treatment and R2R deposition of Cu thin films using a magnetron sputter system. All R2R assembled UCCs exhibited electrical and mechanical properties comparable to those of stationary-processed counterparts, including similar electrical conductivity, ~10% higher current-carrying capacity, and 20% greater tensile strength than those obtained on pure Cu tapes. The technology being developed and scaled here introduces vast application opportunities and immense technological/economic impact in all energy sectors ranging from on- and off-board components in electric drive vehicles to power grid systems, as well as interconnects to electronic devices and data centers.

items.title: Plasma-Enhanced Atomic Layer Deposition and Substrate Engineering of Low-Resistivity Ultrathin MoCx Films for Advanced Interconnect Applications
items.abstract: As Copper (Cu) interconnect dimensions continue to shrink, conventional tantalum/tantalum nitride (Ta/TaN) liner/barrier layers occupy an increasing fraction of the available interconnect volume and introduce additional electrical resistance because of their relatively high resistivity. Therefore, a key challenge is to develop ultrathin liner/barrier materials that can maintain low resistivity while providing effective Cu diffusion-barrier performance. In this work, we demonstrate MoC x as a liner-free barrier material using plasma-enhanced atomic layer deposition (PEALD). For this PEALD-grown film, cycloheptatriene molybdenum tricarbonyl, (η 6 -C 7 H 8 )Mo(CO) 3 , was first introduced as a precursor to synthesize ultrathin molybdenum carbide (MoC x ) films. The effects of plasma reactants, plasma power, deposition temperature, film thickness, and substrate types were systematically evaluated to clarify how PEALD process conditions and substrate chemistry influence the electrical performance of ultrathin MoC x films. We observed nucleation differences during the growth based on the substrate; MoC x films deposited on Al 2 O 3 consistently exhibited lower resistivity than those grown on SiO 2 . Using the optimized deposition process, amorphous MoC x films thinner than 5 nm showed resistivities as low as ~230 μΩ·cm without any post-deposition annealing. For reference, current Ta/TaN liner/barrier layers typically exceed 500 μΩ·cm resistivity in the sub-5 nm thickness regime. Sub-5 nm MoC x film also showed good Cu adhesion and effective Cu diffusion-barrier behavior after thermal annealing of up to 500 °C. These results demonstrate the potential of ultrathin amorphous MoC x as a low-resistivity liner-free barrier material for advanced Cu interconnects.

items.title: Plasma information–based characterization of wedge-shaped bowed etching profile driven by ion dynamics with the tailored voltage waveform bias
items.abstract: Wedge-shaped bowing during high-aspect-ratio Si trench etching under tailored voltage waveform (TVW)-driven dual-frequency capacitively coupled plasma conditions is analyzed from a plasma physics perspective. TVW operation modifies RF sheath dynamics, producing a bi-modal ion energy distribution with an enhanced high-energy component. When reflected from tapered SiO2 mask sidewalls, these ions induce localized energy-flux focusing near the upper trench region, resulting in sharp wedge-shaped profile deformation. Combining in situ diagnostics with feature-scale transport modeling, a plasma-information index, PIBow, is introduced by normalizing the ratio of reflected high-energy ion energy flux to transported O radical flux to a characteristic profile-transition reference scale. This dimensionless index quantifies the competition between ion-driven etching and radical-mediated passivation, and wedge-forming and non-wedge-forming conditions are systematically organized around the normalized reference state PIBow≈1 for the analyzed system. Furthermore, a plasma information–based virtual metrology framework then transforms optical emission spectroscopy and voltage-current sensor measurements into physics-informed plasma variables for wedge geometry prediction. The model reproduces the measured wedge length with a high coefficient of determination (adj. R2 = 0.981) and yields an interpretable process-control window governed by the balance between energetic-ion delivery and O-radical-mediated passivation. An angle-dependent etch rate model is also proposed to describe wedge angle formation, reproducing the measured dependence on the operating conditions. Wedge-shaped bowing thus represents a distinct regime of profile evolution governed by coupled ion dynamics and transport-limited radical supply under TVW conditions, and the methodology presented here offers a scalable framework for understanding, predicting, and engineering plasma–surface interactions in plasma-assisted manufacturing.

items.title: Numerically Stable Small‐Signal Modeling of Highly Linear Composition‐Engineered AlGaN/GaN Fin‐HEMTs Using a Stabilized Berroth‐Based Extraction Methodology
items.abstract: ABSTRACT This work presents a comprehensive TCAD‐to‐RF modeling framework for composition‐engineered multifin AlGaN/GaN HEMTs incorporating fin‐dependent aluminum composition. The proposed device employs asymmetric barrier engineering (AlGaN with across three fins) to simultaneously tailor the threshold voltage and improve linearity while maintaining adequate RF performance. To accurately extract the intrinsic small‐signal parameters, a numerically stable Berroth–Bosch‐based extraction methodology is developed by integrating LOESS‐assisted smoothing, robust mid‐band slope estimation, and physically constrained parameter estimation within the de‐embedding procedure. Unlike conventional extraction techniques, which are susceptible to numerical oscillations and nonphysical parameter values, the proposed methodology consistently yields stable intrinsic parameters enabling reliable evaluation of the RF figures of merit and . Furthermore, robustness against realistic measurement uncertainty is demonstrated through standard‐deviation Gaussian perturbation of the TCAD‐generated S ‐parameters, where the proposed methodology maintains physically meaningful parameter extraction while conventional methods exhibit significant numerical instability. The extracted parameter set represents an equivalent compact small‐signal model of the complete multifin device without increasing circuit complexity as the number of fins increases. The proposed framework provides a reproducible and numerically robust foundation for compact modeling and RF characterization of composition‐engineered multifin GaN HEMTs for high‐frequency integrated circuit applications.
items.venue: International Journal of Numerical Modelling Electronic Networks Devices and Fields

items.title: Negative Activation Energy Under Dynamic Stress of 650 V E-mode GaN HEMTs
items.abstract: We demonstrate for the first time that the process responsible for dynamic R ON degradation in GaN HEMTs operated under application-close SALT hard-switching (HS) conditions exhibits a negative activation energy. This behavior has been attributed to the mitigation of hot-electron-induced degradation at higher temperatures, resulting from the reduced electron mean free path. In addition, a novel real-time in-situ technique to monitor the threshold voltage (V TH ) variation during HS operation is presented. Negligible V TH variation was observed during the tests, along with a significant increase in on-resistance: this result supports the conclusion that hot-electron trapping in the access region is the dominant mechanism responsible for the observed degradation.

items.title: Multi-regime trap dynamics in Si/SiGe/Si MOSFET current transients at cryogenic temperatures
items.abstract: We investigate transient charge-trapping dynamics in Si/SiGe quantum-well MOSFETs at cryogenic temperatures between 𝑇 = 4 K and 𝑇 = 8 0 K . Transient current behavior is analyzed using stress-relaxation measurements inspired by the extended measure–stress–measure (eMSM) technique. The recorded current transients were analyzed by using phenomenological models and extracting corresponding mean relaxation times. A comparison with CV and IV characteristics links these regimes to the activation of different conduction channels in the SiQW/SiCap layers. These results provide new insight into cryogenic trap kinetics relevant for CMOS based Si/SiGe/Si quantum devices.

items.title: Influence of Growing Parameters on Optical Band Gap of Gallium Nitride Deposited on Sapphire by Reactive Magnetron Sputtering
items.abstract: The presented work discusses the preparation of gallium nitride by reactive magnetron sputtering technology and the study of its optical properties. In particular, the dependence of the optical band gap of gallium nitride on technological parameters, such as temperature, UV irradiation and impurity diffusion. The optical band gap was calculated from the emission spectra using the Tauce Plot method. The emission spectra were measured on a UV/VIS/NIR Spectrophotometer Analyzer. The temperature dependence showed an improvement in the band gap with increasing temperature and amounted to 3.37 eV, which is close to the known band gap of gallium nitride of 3.4 eV. The influence of UV irradiation was also studied, which showed a slight improvement in the band gap. In general, UV irradiation improves the structural properties of gallium nitride and, accordingly, was expected to have a positive effect on the optical properties. During magnetron sputtering, silicon as a dopant was mixed, doped. The result showed that doping gallium nitride with silicon reduces the optical band gap by 0.06 eV.

items.title: Enantiomeric separation of rivaroxaban by cyclodextrin-micellar electrokinetic chromatography. Quantitative analysis in pharmaceutical formulations and urine samples.
items.abstract: Background Rivaroxaban is an oral anticoagulant that acts as a direct activated factor X (FXa) inhibitor and is marketed as the enantiomerically pure S-form. The control of its enantiomeric purity is therefore relevant for pharmaceutical quality assessment. This work aimed to develop a Cyclodextrin-Micellar Electrokinetic Chromatography (CD-MEKC) method for the enantiomeric separation and determination of rivaroxaban in pharmaceutical formulations and human urine. Results The optimized CD-MEKC method employed a BGE containing 75 mM 2-(N-morpholino)ethanesulfonic acid (MES) (pH 2.0), 32 mM sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS) and 15 mM methyl-γ-cyclodextrin (M-γ-CD). Under an applied voltage of -25 kV and a capillary temperature of 15 °C, rivaroxaban enantiomers were separated with a resolution of 2.0 within 18 min. The developed methodology showed satisfactory selectivity, linearity, precision, and accuracy (100 ± 6 % in pharmaceutical formulations and 100 ± 3 % in urine samples). Limits of detection (LODs) and quantification (LOQs) were 0.27 and 0.90 mg/L, respectively. The relative LOD for the enantiomeric impurity (R-rivaroxaban) was 0.1% relative to the S-enantiomer. The method was successfully applied to the analysis of a commercial pharmaceutical formulation, showing that the enantiomeric impurity was not detected at the International Council for Harmonisation (ICH) acceptance limit of 0.1 %, and to the chiral determination of rivaroxaban in human urine at therapeutically relevant concentrations. Significance The proposed methodology represents the first approach based on a capillary electromigration technique for the chiral analysis of rivaroxaban and constitutes a simple, cost-effective and low-solvent-consumption analytical tool for pharmaceutical quality control and therapeutic drug monitoring.

items.title: Eco-Friendly Zinc Extraction from Sandy Soils via Electrokinetics Assisted by Tartaric Acid and Agricultural Waste
items.abstract: The contamination of agricultural sandy soils by zinc (Zn) presents not only a risk for the quality of crops but also a problem for the quality of groundwater. Common enhancing agents used in electrokinetic remediation (EKR) of heavy metals, such as EDTA, present persistence in the environment. This work evaluates an EKR technique that involves a biodegradable chelating agent, tartaric acid, and a barrier of untreated rice husk installed in front of the cathode. The experimental design includes a sandy soil (93.4% sand) artificially contaminated with 300 mg/kg Zn and treated for 5 days under the voltage gradient of 1 V/cm. Besides three experiments without enhancement, where the purging solutions were tap water adjusted to pH 3, 7 and 11, there was one experiment with tartaric acid at pH 3 as the anolyte. All experiments were done once. The removal of Zn decreased from 77.8% at pH 3 to 69.7% at pH 7 and 53.2% at pH 11 due to the higher desorption and electromigration of Zn in acidic conditions and the precipitation of Zn as Zn(OH)₂ in neutral and alkaline conditions. In all experiments, the residual amount of Zn decreased along the direction from the anode to the cathode. The removal of Zn in the tartaric acid-enhanced experiment was the highest (90.8%), which corresponds to 13 percentage points more than in the experiment without enhancement at pH 3, with the residual amount of Zn being 15–43 mg/kg in the soil column. This fact is due to the formation of soluble Zn-tartrate complexes and buffering action of tartaric acid that maintained soil pH within 4.2–5.7. The amount of Zn retained in the rice husk barrier was up to 38 mg/kg. Therefore, the EKR enhanced by biodegradable tartaric acid can be considered a potentially useful technique for the remediation of Zn-contaminated sandy soils. Replicate tests, the cost evaluation, the effect of the technique on soil quality and quantification of the barrier contribution are needed.

items.title: Biophysical modeling of iontophoresis-assisted spatially controlled riboflavin delivery in the human cornea
items.abstract: Background and objective Theranostic-guided transepithelial corneal cross-linking uses patterned iontophoresis for minimally invasive, spatially controlled riboflavin delivery in progressive keratoconus. This study developed a computational model to investigate the effects of applied current and reservoir-cornea conformity on riboflavin transport. Methods A 2D axisymmetric finite element model of the layered cornea and a clinically available patterned iontophoresis device was developed. The electric field was coupled to Nernst-Planck equations incorporating diffusion, electromigration, electroosmosis, tissue porosity, and tortuosity. The patterned mask was explicitly modeled, while a conformity parameter accounted for reservoir-cornea contact. Model parameters were constrained using two independent in vivo measurements: the effective electrical resistance of the iontophoresis–cornea system and the volume-averaged stromal riboflavin concentration. Results Electromigration promoted localized transport through mask openings, whereas electroosmosis contributed to deeper stromal penetration; passive diffusion was limited by the intact epithelium. At 420 s, the predicted volume-averaged stromal concentrations across the total treatment region were 97 and 110 μg/cm 3 at 0.5 and 1.0 mA, respectively, consistent with corresponding in vivo measurements of 90 ± 20 and 111 ± 21 μg/cm 3 in 28 keratoconic eyes. The central-to-total concentration ratio increased from 1.95 at 0.5 mA to 2.96 at 2.0 mA, indicating greater spatial selectivity with increasing applied current. Conclusions The model describes transepithelial riboflavin delivery by corneal iontophoresis, highlighting the influence of mask geometry and applied current on spatial riboflavin distribution. Limitations include the 2D axisymmetric approximation, simplified boundary conditions, and lack of direct in vivo validation of riboflavin concentrations at currents above 1.0 mA.

items.title: Side-Channel Attack Prevention for Post Quantum Cryptography Algorithms: A 3D-Shield Approach
items.abstract: Despite their theoretical quantum attack resistance, practical implementations of post-quantum cryptography (PQC) algorithms remain susceptible to side-channel attacks. This includes all standard algorithms selected the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) such as Kyber/ML-KEM, Dilithium/ML-DSA, Falcon/FN-DSA and SPHINCS+/SLH-DSA. This paper proposes an alternative defense for side-channel resilience based on 3D integration that uses 3D hardware to shield the underlying cryptographic activity by introducing decoy keys and physical shielding through stacking. The proposed approach can complement other security measures (such as masking and shuffling) on protecting Number Theoretic Transform (NTT) that move computation to dedicated NTT chips. We outline the construction of our approach and validate the effectiveness on a generic attack targeting intermediate computation inside an NTT butterfly.

items.title: Temperature-dependent operating margins of proton-irradiated integrated 4H-SiC CMOS current mirrors
items.abstract: Integrated 4H-SiC CMOS current mirrors and co-fabricated MOSFETs were characterized at temperatures up to 180 °C and after 15 MeV proton irradiation. The SiC mirrors retain highly linear current transfer over the measured current ranges, with coefficients of determination of 0.99943–0.999996 across the reported conditions. Heating reduces the threshold-voltage magnitude of both NMOS and PMOS devices, whereas irradiation predominantly increases the PMOS threshold-voltage magnitude and the supply voltage required for stable mirroring. Using a common target current ratio of 2.47, the minimum measured supply voltage of the type 2 mirror increases from 7.5 V before irradiation to 10.5 V after a fluence of 5 × 10¹³ cm⁻² at room temperature, and decreases to 9.5 V when the irradiated circuit is measured at 180 °C. Devices annealed in hydrogen before irradiation require higher supply voltages: 12.0 V at room temperature and 10.5 V at 180 °C. These results demonstrate partial, temperature-dependent improvement of the circuit operating margin after irradiation. They do not establish thermal removal of radiation-induced defects. The device and circuit measurements identify threshold-voltage shifts and processing history as relevant considerations for the operating margins of this SiC CMOS platform.

items.title: Streaming Virtual Metrology via Lightweight Adaptation under Temporal Distribution Shifts
items.abstract: Virtual metrology (VM) aims to estimate costly or delayed metrology variables from heterogeneous sensor signals and in-line measurements, and it acts as a critical component of semiconductor manufacturing. While recent data-driven models have improved VM accuracy, most are trained in batch settings and assume stationary data distributions. In practice, however, production environments evolve continuously due to equipment degradation, process adjustments, and maintenance events, making conventional batch-trained VM models difficult to maintain under temporal distribution shifts. In this work, we propose GRAPE (Global Regression with Adaptive Prediction Enhancement), a practical online learning framework for VM in evolving wafer-processing environments. GRAPE integrates a stable global predictor based on interpretable representations with two lightweight streaming adapters that correct feature-level and environment-level shifts through online updates. Experiments on two real-world semiconductor manufacturing datasets, including chronologically held-out blind-test streams, show that GRAPE improves robustness and generalization under real temporal drift compared with both conventional batch-learning methods and existing online learning baselines.

items.title: Source-feedback and thermal-uniformity co-design of a multi-chip SiC MOSFET module
items.abstract: Multi-chip paralleled silicon carbide (SiC) MOSFET power modules require package layouts that control both switching-induced source feedback and chip-level heat-flow nonuniformity.
